fullTitle: Practice Exam 3: AWS Certified Machine Learning Engineer Associate (MLA-C01)

questions.promptHtml: A pharmaceutical discovery lab's ML platform team keeps a curated feature dataset on Amazon EFS. The dataset is used by multiple preprocessing containers and notebooks that expect a shared file system path and update files between experiments. The team needs an Amazon SageMaker training job to read the dataset without first copying it into Amazon S3. The training job can run in the required VPC. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST data movement?
questions.promptText:
A pharmaceutical discovery lab's ML platform team keeps a curated feature dataset on Amazon EFS. The dataset is used by multiple preprocessing containers and notebooks that expect a shared file system path and update files between experiments. The team needs an Amazon SageMaker training job to read the dataset without first copying it into Amazon S3. The training job can run in the required VPC.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST data movement?

options.text: Copy the dataset to an Amazon EBS Provisioned IOPS volume and run a self-managed Amazon EC2 training workload.
Enable Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration and upload the dataset to an S3 bucket before starting each training job.
Configure the SageMaker training job to use the Amazon EFS file system as the training data source in the VPC.
Export the dataset to Amazon S3 by using a database snapshot export and point SageMaker to the exported files.

correctText: Configure the SageMaker training job to use the Amazon EFS file system as the training data source in the VPC.
questions.explanationHtml:
For SageMaker training, the best data access method depends on where the training data already lives and how the training code reads it. When a dataset is already on Amazon EFS, and the job can run in the needed VPC, configuring the training job to use EFS avoids an unnecessary extraction and staging step. This is a good fit for file based workflows that expect a shared file system path rather than object storage semantics.

Amazon S3 is the most common source for SageMaker training data, and SageMaker supports multiple S3 input modes, including File, FastFile, and Pipe. Those modes are useful when the data is stored in S3, but moving an existing EFS dataset into S3 just to start training adds operational overhead and data movement. Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration helps with long distance S3 transfers, but it does not remove the need to upload the data into S3 first.

Amazon EBS Provisioned IOPS is block storage for workloads that need predictable IOPS and low latency, but using it here would require a different compute pattern or additional staging instead of configuring the existing EFS dataset as the SageMaker training data source. Database snapshot export is also the wrong pattern here because it is designed for exporting database snapshot data into S3, not for reading an existing EFS based feature dataset. For more information, see Access Training Data, Amazon EFS Performance, Configuring fast, secure file transfers using Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration, and Amazon EBS Provisioned IOPS SSD volumes.

questions.promptHtml: A regional grocery cooperative's pricing analytics team trains an XGBoost model in Amazon SageMaker to predict product demand. The model artifact has grown large enough that deployment tests require more endpoint memory than expected. The team wants to reduce the stored model footprint without changing the source data location or moving to a larger hosting instance. Which action will MOST directly meet this requirement?
questions.promptText:
A regional grocery cooperative's pricing analytics team trains an XGBoost model in Amazon SageMaker to predict product demand. The model artifact has grown large enough that deployment tests require more endpoint memory than expected. The team wants to reduce the stored model footprint without changing the source data location or moving to a larger hosting instance.

Which action will MOST directly meet this requirement?

options.text: Add more engineered categorical features and rerun automatic model tuning with wider ranges.
Increase the SageMaker training instance memory and keep the same XGBoost hyperparameters.
Constrain the XGBoost model complexity by reducing tree depth and limiting boosting rounds.
Switch the SageMaker training input from file mode to pipe mode without changing training settings.

correctText: Constrain the XGBoost model complexity by reducing tree depth and limiting boosting rounds.
questions.explanationHtml:
Model size is driven by what must be stored for inference, not just by how much raw training data was used. For tree-based models such as XGBoost, the trained artifact stores the learned tree ensemble, so factors such as the number of boosting rounds, tree depth, and other complexity controls can affect the footprint. The SageMaker XGBoost documentation lists hyperparameters such as num_round, max_depth, and related complexity settings that shape the trained model, see XGBoost Hyperparameters.

Choosing a larger instance can mask the symptom by providing more memory, but it does not address the underlying model artifact size. Similarly, changing the way data is streamed into training affects the training data path, not the complexity of the learned model. A useful mental model is that a model artifact contains learned parameters, definitions, and metadata, as described in ModelArtifacts, so reducing footprint usually means reducing what the model has learned and must store.

questions.domain: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.promptHtml: An airline revenue optimization team stores raw booking datasets, training outputs, and approved SageMaker model artifacts in separate prefixes of the same Amazon S3 bucket. Data scientists must be able to create SageMaker model resources only from the approved model artifact prefix. The team also wants to prevent data scientists from selecting arbitrary SageMaker execution roles during model creation. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST privilege?
questions.promptText:
An airline revenue optimization team stores raw booking datasets, training outputs, and approved SageMaker model artifacts in separate prefixes of the same Amazon S3 bucket. Data scientists must be able to create SageMaker model resources only from the approved model artifact prefix. The team also wants to prevent data scientists from selecting arbitrary SageMaker execution roles during model creation.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST privilege?

options.text: Create a dedicated SageMaker execution role with read access to the approved artifact prefix, and allow iam:PassRole only for that role.
Create an S3 bucket policy that allows each data scientist to read the entire bucket, and deny delete actions on the bucket.
Attach AmazonSageMakerFullAccess to each data scientist, and allow iam:PassRole for all SageMaker execution roles in the account.
Store approved artifacts in a separate S3 prefix, and rely on SageMaker Model Registry approvals to restrict S3 object access.

correctText: Create a dedicated SageMaker execution role with read access to the approved artifact prefix, and allow iam:PassRole only for that role.
questions.explanationHtml:
For SageMaker model creation, there are two related permission boundaries to think about: what the human or automation principal can ask SageMaker to do, and what the SageMaker execution role can access when SageMaker performs work on the user's behalf. Least privilege usually requires controlling both. If a user can pass any execution role, that user might indirectly gain access to data that the user's own identity policy does not allow.

The correct design is to create a narrowly scoped SageMaker execution role that can read only the approved model artifact location in Amazon S3, then allow users to pass only that role with iam:PassRole. If the artifacts are encrypted with a customer managed KMS key, the same least-privilege idea applies to the key permissions as well. The role should receive only the decrypt permissions needed for the approved artifact workflow.

Broad managed policies such as full SageMaker access can be useful during early development, but they are an anti-pattern for production least privilege when the required actions and resources are known. S3 bucket-wide read access is also too broad when approved artifacts, raw data, and training outputs share a bucket. Lifecycle controls such as Model Registry approvals are valuable for governance, but they do not enforce S3 object authorization by themselves.

For more information, see SageMaker AI execution roles, SageMaker AI identity-based policy examples, and Amazon S3 access policy language overview.

questions.promptHtml: A medical device manufacturer's quality engineering team is training a model in Amazon SageMaker AI to inspect assembly-line images. Each image can contain several visible defects, and the team needs the model to identify every defect instance in the image and assign a defect category with a confidence score. The team wants to use a SageMaker AI built-in algorithm instead of maintaining custom training code. Which approach should the team use?
questions.promptText:
A medical device manufacturer's quality engineering team is training a model in Amazon SageMaker AI to inspect assembly-line images. Each image can contain several visible defects, and the team needs the model to identify every defect instance in the image and assign a defect category with a confidence score. The team wants to use a SageMaker AI built-in algorithm instead of maintaining custom training code.

Which approach should the team use?

options.text: Train the SageMaker AI Object Detection built-in algorithm on labeled defect images.
Train the SageMaker AI Image Classification built-in algorithm on labeled defect images.
Train a SageMaker AI Scikit-learn estimator with a logistic regression script.
Train the SageMaker AI Linear Learner built-in algorithm on flattened image pixels.

correctText: Train the SageMaker AI Object Detection built-in algorithm on labeled defect images.
questions.explanationHtml:
For a vision task where an image can contain multiple object instances, the mental model should be detection rather than whole-image classification. SageMaker AI built-in algorithms include options for common problem types, and object detection is the appropriate built-in algorithm when the model must find instances in an image and associate each with a category and confidence score. See the SageMaker AI built-in algorithm overview in Use Amazon SageMaker built-in algorithms or pretrained models.

Image classification is useful when the question is, what is the main class of this image? It does not naturally satisfy a requirement to identify every visible defect instance in one image. Linear Learner and a Scikit-learn logistic regression script can solve many tabular classification problems, but they are poor fits for this spatial computer vision task and would require feature engineering or custom code that the team is trying to avoid. SageMaker AI also supports training with built-in algorithms, framework estimators, and custom containers, as described in Train a model with Amazon SageMaker.

questions.promptHtml: A film streaming service's personalization team has a TensorFlow training script and several helper Python files in a source repository. The training data is stored in Amazon S3. The team wants to run repeatable GPU training jobs on Amazon SageMaker AI managed training infrastructure, write model artifacts to Amazon S3, and avoid building or maintaining a custom Docker image. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
A film streaming service's personalization team has a TensorFlow training script and several helper Python files in a source repository. The training data is stored in Amazon S3. The team wants to run repeatable GPU training jobs on Amazon SageMaker AI managed training infrastructure, write model artifacts to Amazon S3, and avoid building or maintaining a custom Docker image.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Package the TensorFlow script into a custom Docker image, push the image to Amazon ECR, and create a SageMaker AI estimator that uses the custom image URI.
Upload the TensorFlow script to a SageMaker AI notebook instance, install the helper packages manually, and run the training process directly inside the notebook kernel.
Choose a SageMaker AI built-in algorithm container, place the TensorFlow script in the S3 training data prefix, and start a training job that points to that prefix.
Create a SageMaker AI TensorFlow estimator that specifies the training script as the entry point, include the helper files as source code, and call fit with the Amazon S3 training data location.

correctText: Create a SageMaker AI TensorFlow estimator that specifies the training script as the entry point, include the helper files as source code, and call fit with the Amazon S3 training data location.
questions.explanationHtml:
Script mode is the managed SageMaker AI path for running custom Python training code with supported frameworks such as TensorFlow and PyTorch. Instead of building a container, the ML engineer provides an entry_point script, optional source files or dependencies, framework and Python versions, instance configuration, and the Amazon S3 locations for data and output.

The supported framework estimator uses a prebuilt SageMaker AI framework container, starts a managed training job, makes the training data available to the job, runs the user script, and persists model artifacts to Amazon S3. This gives the team the control of custom training code while avoiding the operational work of creating and maintaining a Docker image.

A custom Docker image is appropriate when the required runtime, libraries, or serving behavior cannot be satisfied by the supported containers, but it is not the least overhead choice here. Running training inside a notebook is also an anti-pattern for repeatable managed training because the notebook becomes the execution environment rather than a managed training job. Built-in algorithms are useful when their algorithm matches the problem, but they are not a mechanism for running arbitrary TensorFlow code.

For more information, see Use machine learning frameworks, Python, and R with Amazon SageMaker AI, Use TensorFlow with Amazon SageMaker AI, and Docker containers with SageMaker AI.

questions.promptHtml: A city transit authority's ridership analytics group stores raw fare-card exports, customer-service notes, and station survey files in Amazon S3. Before creating training datasets, the governance team must identify which S3 objects likely contain personally identifiable information (PII) and generate findings for review. The team does not need to produce a masked copy yet and wants minimal custom code. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
A city transit authority's ridership analytics group stores raw fare-card exports, customer-service notes, and station survey files in Amazon S3. Before creating training datasets, the governance team must identify which S3 objects likely contain personally identifiable information (PII) and generate findings for review. The team does not need to produce a masked copy yet and wants minimal custom code.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Enable Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery on the S3 buckets and review the generated findings.
Use Amazon Comprehend to redact PII from each text document before storing the result in S3.
Apply AWS Lake Formation data filters to restrict columns that contain sensitive fields.
Run an AWS Glue Detect PII transform and write redacted records to a separate S3 location.

correctText: Enable Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery on the S3 buckets and review the generated findings.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon Macie is the best fit when the first task is to discover and classify sensitive data in Amazon S3. Macie uses machine learning and pattern matching to help identify data such as PII, and it reports findings that a governance or security team can review before ML engineers decide how to cleanse, mask, or remove the data. See Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery in S3.

Data preparation tools such as AWS Glue and AWS Glue DataBrew are more appropriate when the team is ready to transform data, for example by redacting, hashing, deleting, or masking sensitive fields. Those tools can be part of a later sanitization pipeline, but they are not the lowest overhead choice when the immediate requirement is S3 sensitive data discovery and findings. See AWS Glue Detect PII transform and AWS Glue DataBrew personal information protection.

Lake Formation is a governance control plane for cataloged data, including tag-based permissions and row, column, or cell-level filters. It is useful after sensitive data is known and cataloged, but it does not replace the discovery step for raw S3 objects. Amazon Comprehend can detect or redact PII in text documents, but using it directly requires a document processing workflow rather than managed S3-wide classification findings.

questions.promptHtml: A retail media network's data engineering team receives a steady stream of ad impression events from store kiosks. Events arrive as CSV records and must be converted to JSON, batched to reduce outbound calls, and delivered near real time to a partner analytics platform through an HTTPS endpoint. The transformation is stateless, and the team wants a serverless option that minimizes custom application code. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A retail media network's data engineering team receives a steady stream of ad impression events from store kiosks. Events arrive as CSV records and must be converted to JSON, batched to reduce outbound calls, and delivered near real time to a partner analytics platform through an HTTPS endpoint. The transformation is stateless, and the team wants a serverless option that minimizes custom application code.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure an Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream with an AWS Lambda transformation and a custom HTTP endpoint destination.
Configure an AWS Glue streaming ETL job with Spark Structured Streaming and custom HTTPS delivery code.
Configure an Amazon Kinesis Data Streams stream with an AWS Lambda consumer and custom HTTPS delivery code.
Configure an Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink application with custom HTTPS delivery code.

correctText: Configure an Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream with an AWS Lambda transformation and a custom HTTP endpoint destination.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon Data Firehose is built for managed streaming delivery rather than long-running custom consumer applications. It can buffer incoming records, invoke AWS Lambda to transform source data, and then deliver the transformed data to supported destinations such as Amazon S3, Amazon OpenSearch Service, and custom HTTP endpoints. For this scenario, that means the team can focus on the small CSV-to-JSON transformation while Firehose manages the delivery pipeline. See Transform source data in Amazon Data Firehose.

Kinesis Data Streams with Lambda is a valid pattern when an application needs direct stream consumption, custom processing, or control over how records are handled. Lambda can be invoked from a Kinesis stream, as described in Using AWS Lambda with Amazon Kinesis, but the team would still own more of the downstream delivery behavior. That extra control is useful in some systems, but it is not the lowest-overhead choice for managed batching and delivery to an HTTPS endpoint.

AWS Glue streaming ETL and Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink are better aligned with richer stream processing requirements. Glue streaming jobs use Spark streaming concepts, and Flink is appropriate for custom streaming applications that need more advanced processing semantics. Those services are powerful, but for a stateless record conversion followed by managed near real-time delivery, they are more complex than necessary. See AWS Glue streaming concepts and Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink Documentation.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: A maritime logistics firm's ML engineering team has trained a model in Amazon SageMaker AI to predict container inspection risk. Port gate applications send individual scoring requests continuously during operating hours, require responses in the application request path, and cannot tolerate cold-start delays. A compliance team also uploads a large scoring dataset each night and only needs the completed predictions before the next morning. The team wants to use managed SageMaker inference options without building custom hosting code. Which two actions should the team take? (Select TWO.)
questions.promptText:
A maritime logistics firm's ML engineering team has trained a model in Amazon SageMaker AI to predict container inspection risk. Port gate applications send individual scoring requests continuously during operating hours, require responses in the application request path, and cannot tolerate cold-start delays. A compliance team also uploads a large scoring dataset each night and only needs the completed predictions before the next morning. The team wants to use managed SageMaker inference options without building custom hosting code.

Which two actions should the team take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Run the model in Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate for both managed scoring workflows.
Deploy the model to a SageMaker real-time endpoint for synchronous port gate scoring requests.
Use SageMaker Asynchronous Inference for synchronous port gate scoring requests.
Run a SageMaker Batch Transform job for the nightly compliance scoring dataset.
Deploy the model to a SageMaker serverless endpoint for the nightly compliance scoring dataset.

correctText: Deploy the model to a SageMaker real-time endpoint for synchronous port gate scoring requests.
Run a SageMaker Batch Transform job for the nightly compliance scoring dataset.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker real-time endpoints are the right fit when an application sends individual requests and needs an immediate prediction in the response path. They provide managed HTTPS endpoints for low-latency inference, and they can be monitored and scaled as traffic changes. For the port gate application, a persistent real-time endpoint is a better match than serverless inference because the scenario states that cold starts are not acceptable. See Overview of Amazon SageMaker AI real-time inference.

SageMaker Batch Transform is designed for offline scoring of datasets. Instead of keeping an endpoint running, SageMaker provisions resources for the transform job, reads the input data, writes prediction output, and then the job completes. This makes it appropriate for a nightly compliance dataset where the business requirement is a completed output file by the next morning, not an immediate response for each record. See SageMaker Batch Transform.

Asynchronous inference and serverless inference are useful SageMaker options, but they optimize for different tradeoffs. Asynchronous inference is for queued requests with large payloads or longer processing times, while serverless inference reduces infrastructure management for intermittent endpoint traffic that can tolerate cold starts. Choosing among these options is mostly about matching latency, request shape, payload size, and operational overhead to the workload instead of defaulting every model to a persistent endpoint.

questions.domain: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.promptHtml: An online education provider's student success team hosts an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint that predicts which learners need academic outreach. The endpoint captures inference inputs and predictions. The team recently expanded into a new market and wants alerts if the factors influencing model predictions begin to change compared with the approved training baseline. Final course completion outcomes will not be available until the end of the semester. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST custom monitoring code?
questions.promptText:
An online education provider's student success team hosts an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint that predicts which learners need academic outreach. The endpoint captures inference inputs and predictions. The team recently expanded into a new market and wants alerts if the factors influencing model predictions begin to change compared with the approved training baseline. Final course completion outcomes will not be available until the end of the semester.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST custom monitoring code?

options.text: Configure SageMaker Model Monitor model quality monitoring to compare predictions with labels and publish alerts to CloudWatch.
Configure SageMaker Model Monitor data quality monitoring to baseline feature statistics and publish drift alerts to CloudWatch.
Configure recurring SageMaker Pipelines retraining jobs to refresh the model monthly and publish job status alerts to CloudWatch.
Configure SageMaker Model Monitor with SageMaker Clarify to baseline feature attributions and publish drift alerts to CloudWatch.

correctText: Configure SageMaker Model Monitor with SageMaker Clarify to baseline feature attributions and publish drift alerts to CloudWatch.
questions.explanationHtml:
Drift can mean several different things in an ML system. Input feature distributions can drift, model accuracy can drift when labels show that predictions are getting worse, bias metrics can drift across groups, and the relative importance of features can drift. In this scenario, the team is not asking whether raw feature values changed or whether accuracy has already degraded. The team wants to know whether the factors influencing predictions are changing.

SageMaker Model Monitor provides managed monitoring jobs for deployed models and can publish monitoring results to CloudWatch for alerting. For this requirement, the appropriate monitoring type is feature attribution drift, which uses SageMaker Clarify capabilities to compare feature attribution behavior from a baseline against live inference data. See the SageMaker Model Monitor overview at Overview of Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor and the feature attribution drift documentation at Monitor feature attribution drift for models in production.

Data quality monitoring is useful when the question is about whether production feature statistics differ from a baseline, but that is a lower level signal than prediction drivers. Model quality monitoring is useful when ground truth labels are available and the team wants to track metrics such as accuracy or error over time, as described in Monitor model quality. Scheduled retraining can be part of a response plan, but it should generally be triggered by measured degradation or drift rather than used as a substitute for observability.

questions.domain: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.promptHtml: A wind energy operator's predictive maintenance team hosts a sensor anomaly model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. During daily turbine upload windows, the endpoint meets throughput targets but latency exceeds the operations team's threshold. The team wants to compare multiple endpoint configurations under the expected traffic pattern before changing production, and wants to minimize custom load testing code. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?
questions.promptText:
A wind energy operator's predictive maintenance team hosts a sensor anomaly model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. During daily turbine upload windows, the endpoint meets throughput targets but latency exceeds the operations team's threshold. The team wants to compare multiple endpoint configurations under the expected traffic pattern before changing production, and wants to minimize custom load testing code.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational effort?

options.text: Move the model to SageMaker Batch Transform and schedule predictions after each upload window.
Increase the endpoint variant maximum instance count and configure target tracking auto scaling.
Configure SageMaker Model Monitor and create CloudWatch alarms for data quality constraint violations.
Register the model in SageMaker Model Registry and run a SageMaker Inference Recommender endpoint recommendation job.

correctText: Register the model in SageMaker Model Registry and run a SageMaker Inference Recommender endpoint recommendation job.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker Inference Recommender is designed for the situation where an ML team needs empirical evidence about how a model behaves on different hosting configurations. Instead of writing and maintaining a custom load test harness, the team can register the model and run recommendation jobs that evaluate endpoint configurations against workload expectations such as traffic shape, latency, and throughput. The output helps engineers make a practical tradeoff among cost, model latency, and invocations supported by a configuration.

Auto scaling and CloudWatch remain important after deployment. CloudWatch provides endpoint metrics such as invocation and latency related metrics, and SageMaker endpoint auto scaling can adjust capacity as traffic changes. However, auto scaling does not answer the earlier sizing question by itself: whether a different instance family, instance size, or starting configuration would meet the latency threshold more efficiently.

Model Monitor solves a different operational problem. It helps detect data quality drift, model quality degradation, bias drift, and feature attribution drift, which are about the statistical behavior of inputs and predictions rather than endpoint capacity benchmarking. Batch Transform is also the wrong fit when the application needs a real-time serving pattern, because it is optimized for offline inference over datasets rather than low-latency request handling.

For more information, see Create recommendation jobs for Amazon SageMaker Inference Recommender, Monitor Amazon SageMaker with Amazon CloudWatch, and Automatically scale Amazon SageMaker models.

questions.promptHtml: A precision agriculture analytics team trains an image segmentation model in Amazon SageMaker AI. The training images are stored in Amazon S3, and the training script expects a POSIX-style directory tree with many small random reads during each epoch. The current S3 File mode setup spends too much time staging data before training starts. The team can run the training job in a VPC and wants high-throughput, low-latency file access while keeping Amazon S3 as the durable data repository. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST change to the training code?
questions.promptText:
A precision agriculture analytics team trains an image segmentation model in Amazon SageMaker AI. The training images are stored in Amazon S3, and the training script expects a POSIX-style directory tree with many small random reads during each epoch. The current S3 File mode setup spends too much time staging data before training starts. The team can run the training job in a VPC and wants high-throughput, low-latency file access while keeping Amazon S3 as the durable data repository.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST change to the training code?

options.text: Configure S3 Fast File mode for the S3 input channel, and keep the existing SageMaker training job pointed directly at the S3 bucket.
Use Amazon Data Firehose to deliver the image tiles into a new S3 prefix, and configure SageMaker File mode to read from that prefix.
Mount an Amazon EFS file system for the input channel, and copy the image tiles from S3 into the file system before every training job.
Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system linked to the S3 bucket, and configure the SageMaker training job to read from the file system.

correctText: Create an Amazon FSx for Lustre file system linked to the S3 bucket, and configure the SageMaker training job to read from the file system.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon FSx for Lustre is the best fit when SageMaker training needs a high-performance file system for large-scale ML or HPC-style workloads. It provides file system semantics with very high throughput and low latency, and it can integrate with Amazon S3 so that data in S3 can be accessed through the file system instead of being copied into each training container first.

SageMaker training can use several data access patterns, including S3 File mode, S3 Fast File mode, Amazon EFS, and Amazon FSx for Lustre. S3 Fast File mode is useful when the goal is to avoid waiting for a full S3 download before training starts, but the course guidance notes that it works best with sequential access. For many small random reads and a script that expects a directory tree, a file system optimized for parallel workloads is a stronger match.

Amazon EFS can also be used with SageMaker training, but it is most appropriate when the training data is already in EFS and the workload does not require the high-throughput parallel file system characteristics of FSx for Lustre. The important operational requirement is that file-system-based SageMaker inputs require VPC connectivity to the file system. For more detail, see Overview of SageMaker AI training data access options and Use Amazon FSx for Lustre as a training data source.

questions.domain: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.promptHtml: A pharmaceutical safety analytics team runs an Amazon SageMaker processing job that builds model features from large clinical event tables. The job repeatedly slows during in-memory joins and sometimes fails before writing the transformed data to Amazon S3. CloudWatch metrics and job logs show memory saturation on the processing instances while CPU utilization remains moderate. The team wants to improve job stability without changing the data processing code or adding GPU acceleration. Which action should the team take?
questions.promptText:
A pharmaceutical safety analytics team runs an Amazon SageMaker processing job that builds model features from large clinical event tables. The job repeatedly slows during in-memory joins and sometimes fails before writing the transformed data to Amazon S3. CloudWatch metrics and job logs show memory saturation on the processing instances while CPU utilization remains moderate. The team wants to improve job stability without changing the data processing code or adding GPU acceleration.

Which action should the team take?

options.text: Move the processing job to a memory optimized instance family and rerun performance tests.
Move the processing job to a general purpose instance family and rerun performance tests.
Move the processing job to an accelerated computing instance family and rerun performance tests.
Move the processing job to a compute optimized instance family and rerun performance tests.

correctText: Move the processing job to a memory optimized instance family and rerun performance tests.
questions.explanationHtml:
An instance type determines the hardware resources available to a workload, including CPU, memory, storage, networking, and accelerator capabilities. When monitoring shows that a workload is constrained by one resource, the right operational response is to choose an instance family that increases that constrained resource and then validate performance with testing.

In this scenario, the critical clue is memory saturation during in-memory joins while CPU utilization remains moderate. A memory optimized instance family is the best fit because the processing job needs more RAM to hold working data structures, cached data, or join state. A compute optimized instance would make more sense for a CPU-bound preprocessing job, and accelerated computing would make more sense for workloads that can use GPUs or ML accelerators.

SageMaker and EC2 both expose multiple instance families so engineers can match workload behavior to hardware characteristics rather than selecting instances by size alone. AWS recommends evaluating hardware choices based on workload needs and validating with tests, as described in Amazon EC2 Instance Types and Amazon SageMaker AI Instance Types.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: A laboratory automation startup's ML platform team trains and hosts a PyTorch model on Amazon SageMaker AI. The model code depends on a proprietary C++ feature extraction library that must be installed in the runtime image with native system dependencies. The team wants to retain SageMaker-managed training and hosting while minimizing ongoing container maintenance. Which container approach should the team use?
questions.promptText:
A laboratory automation startup's ML platform team trains and hosts a PyTorch model on Amazon SageMaker AI. The model code depends on a proprietary C++ feature extraction library that must be installed in the runtime image with native system dependencies. The team wants to retain SageMaker-managed training and hosting while minimizing ongoing container maintenance.

Which container approach should the team use?

options.text: Extend a SageMaker-provided PyTorch container with the proprietary library, publish the image to Amazon ECR, and configure SageMaker jobs and endpoints to use it.
Build a Docker image from a minimal Linux base image, implement the SageMaker container contract, and configure SageMaker jobs and endpoints to use it.
Use an unmodified SageMaker-provided PyTorch container, place the proprietary library in the model artifact, and configure SageMaker jobs and endpoints to load it.
Package the PyTorch code in an Amazon ECS Fargate task, store the image in Amazon ECR, and invoke the task from the ML workflow.

correctText: Extend a SageMaker-provided PyTorch container with the proprietary library, publish the image to Amazon ECR, and configure SageMaker jobs and endpoints to use it.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon SageMaker AI runs training and inference workloads in Docker containers. When the model uses a common framework such as PyTorch, a SageMaker-provided framework container is usually the lowest-maintenance starting point because it already includes the expected framework runtime and SageMaker integration behavior. AWS documentation describes this decision path in SageMaker container decision guidance and summarizes available pre-built images in Use pre-built SageMaker Docker images.

When extra runtime dependencies are required, especially native libraries or operating system packages, the practical pattern is to extend a pre-built container. The team can build a derived image that installs the proprietary C++ library, push that image to Amazon ECR, and reference it from SageMaker training jobs or model hosting configuration. This preserves the benefits of SageMaker-managed training and endpoints without forcing the team to implement every container detail from scratch.

A fully custom container is appropriate when the provided framework images cannot be adapted, for example when using an unusual runtime or a specialized model server. In this scenario, the team explicitly wants to use existing PyTorch support where possible, so a from-scratch image is unnecessarily heavy. Putting native dependencies in the model artifact is also the wrong mental model, because the container image supplies the runtime environment while the model artifact supplies trained model files.

questions.promptHtml: A consumer lending cooperative's risk modeling team trains an XGBoost binary classifier in Amazon SageMaker AI by using automatic model tuning. Several earlier tuning jobs used the same training data and algorithm but were stopped before the team reached the target recall. The training jobs emit the objective metric iteratively during training. The team wants a new tuning run that uses the previous search results and reduces compute spent on trials that are unlikely to improve the objective. Which TWO actions should the team take?
questions.promptText:
A consumer lending cooperative's risk modeling team trains an XGBoost binary classifier in Amazon SageMaker AI by using automatic model tuning. Several earlier tuning jobs used the same training data and algorithm but were stopped before the team reached the target recall. The training jobs emit the objective metric iteratively during training. The team wants a new tuning run that uses the previous search results and reduces compute spent on trials that are unlikely to improve the objective.

Which TWO actions should the team take?

options.text: Use a warm start with the IDENTICAL_DATA_AND_ALGORITHM type.
Use grid search across every categorical value in the parameter space.
Enable automatic early stopping in the tuning job configuration.
Add every available algorithm hyperparameter to the tunable range configuration.
Increase maximum parallel training jobs and run random search for all trials.

correctText: Use a warm start with the IDENTICAL_DATA_AND_ALGORITHM type.
Enable automatic early stopping in the tuning job configuration.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon SageMaker AI Automatic Model Tuning runs multiple training jobs over specified hyperparameter ranges and selects the best result based on an objective metric. The engineer should think of AMT as a managed search process: the more intelligently the search uses signals from prior and current trials, the less compute is wasted on unlikely candidates. See Overview of Amazon SageMaker AI Automatic Model Tuning and Define metrics for Amazon SageMaker automatic model tuning.

Early stopping is appropriate when training emits the objective metric iteratively, such as after each epoch or training round. It lets AMT stop poor performing training jobs before they consume the full planned training time. Warm start is the matching capability for reusing knowledge from previous tuning jobs, and IDENTICAL_DATA_AND_ALGORITHM is the relevant warm start type when the earlier jobs used the same dataset and algorithm. The API supports these tuning job settings, as described in CreateHyperParameterTuningJob.

Grid search, broad random search, and tuning every available hyperparameter are common anti-patterns when the goal is efficient optimization. Grid search is brute force, random search does not depend on prior runs, and adding unnecessary hyperparameters makes the search space explode. A practical AMT integration usually combines a clear objective metric, a focused set of important hyperparameters, and efficiency features such as early stopping and warm start when the scenario supports them. For strategy context, see How hyperparameter tuning works.

questions.domain: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.promptHtml: A concert ticketing platform's fraud analytics team retrains an Amazon SageMaker model from curated files in an Amazon S3 bucket. An existing SageMaker Pipeline performs the retraining. The team must keep an audit trail of object-level write activity to the training bucket and must start the retraining pipeline automatically when new curated files are written. The team wants to avoid polling S3 or writing a custom scheduler. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A concert ticketing platform's fraud analytics team retrains an Amazon SageMaker model from curated files in an Amazon S3 bucket. An existing SageMaker Pipeline performs the retraining. The team must keep an audit trail of object-level write activity to the training bucket and must start the retraining pipeline automatically when new curated files are written. The team wants to avoid polling S3 or writing a custom scheduler.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Enable CloudTrail S3 data events for write activity on the training bucket, deliver the trail to S3, and use an EventBridge rule to start the SageMaker Pipeline.
Enable CloudTrail Insights for the training account, send Insights events to EventBridge, and use an EventBridge target to start the SageMaker Pipeline.
Use the default CloudTrail management events for the training bucket, deliver the trail to S3, and use a CloudWatch alarm to start the SageMaker Pipeline.
Configure S3 Event Notifications for object-created events, invoke a Lambda function to start the SageMaker Pipeline, and rely on Lambda logs for auditing.

correctText: Enable CloudTrail S3 data events for write activity on the training bucket, deliver the trail to S3, and use an EventBridge rule to start the SageMaker Pipeline.
questions.explanationHtml:
AWS CloudTrail is the right service when the requirement is to audit API activity, including who called an API, when it was called, and which resource was affected. For S3 object-level operations such as writes to training data, the relevant CloudTrail category is data events, which are high-volume events and are not logged by default. A trail can deliver those events to Amazon S3 for audit retention, while Amazon EventBridge can react to CloudTrail API-call events without requiring a polling process.

For an ML retraining workflow, EventBridge provides the automation layer and SageMaker Pipelines provides the repeatable retraining process. The mental model is: CloudTrail records the API activity, EventBridge matches the event pattern, and SageMaker Pipelines runs the controlled training workflow. CloudWatch is better suited for metrics, logs, dashboards, and alarms, while CloudTrail Insights is for anomalous management-event patterns rather than every normal data change. For more information, see AWS CloudTrail overview, EventBridge events delivered via CloudTrail, and SageMaker Pipelines with EventBridge.

questions.domain: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.promptHtml: A sports analytics lab's ML workspace team uses Amazon SageMaker Studio notebooks to build models from confidential player telemetry stored in private databases and Amazon S3. The security team requires all Studio app traffic to use the lab's controlled VPC networking path so that access can be limited with private subnets and security groups. Users must still be able to reach approved AWS resources needed for training and hosting. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A sports analytics lab's ML workspace team uses Amazon SageMaker Studio notebooks to build models from confidential player telemetry stored in private databases and Amazon S3. The security team requires all Studio app traffic to use the lab's controlled VPC networking path so that access can be limited with private subnets and security groups. Users must still be able to reach approved AWS resources needed for training and hosting.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create the SageMaker AI Domain with VPC Only network access, specify private subnets and security groups, and provide approved VPC endpoints or controlled NAT access.
Enable network isolation only on SageMaker training jobs, keep Studio default network access, and grant users private database permissions through IAM policies.
Create the SageMaker AI Domain in public subnets, attach an internet gateway route, and limit inbound access with a security group on the domain apps.
Create the SageMaker AI Domain with default network access, restrict notebook IAM permissions, and rely on CloudTrail to audit external connections.

correctText: Create the SageMaker AI Domain with VPC Only network access, specify private subnets and security groups, and provide approved VPC endpoints or controlled NAT access.
questions.explanationHtml:
For SageMaker Studio environments that must be isolated, the important design choice is to put the workspace traffic under the customer's VPC controls rather than leaving it on a default internet-enabled path. A VPC spans Availability Zones, while subnets are placed in specific Availability Zones, so private subnets let teams decide which routes are available to Studio apps and related resources. See Amazon VPC basics for the VPC and subnet model.

Security groups operate as stateful virtual firewalls for associated resources, which makes them a natural control point for least-privilege access to private databases, endpoints, and other internal services. The SageMaker configuration should specify the VPC subnets and security groups that the jobs or apps use, then add only the connectivity needed for approved AWS services, such as VPC endpoints or a controlled NAT path where appropriate. See Security groups and Give SageMaker AI access to resources in your Amazon VPC.

Auditing services such as CloudTrail are valuable, but they do not enforce private routing. Similarly, public subnets and internet gateways are the opposite of a private isolation pattern. Network isolation for a training container is a narrower SageMaker setting, it does not by itself solve Studio domain traffic control and can affect access to required data sources if the surrounding VPC design is incomplete.

questions.promptHtml: An urban transit authority's fare optimization team is preparing features for a model that predicts station crowding. Turnstile events are uploaded hourly as CSV files to Amazon S3. Station attributes and service calendars are stored in a JDBC-compatible relational database. The team must join the datasets by station ID and service date, remove duplicate rows, and write a curated Parquet dataset to Amazon S3 for Athena queries and model training. The process must run every night with minimal infrastructure administration. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
An urban transit authority's fare optimization team is preparing features for a model that predicts station crowding. Turnstile events are uploaded hourly as CSV files to Amazon S3. Station attributes and service calendars are stored in a JDBC-compatible relational database. The team must join the datasets by station ID and service date, remove duplicate rows, and write a curated Parquet dataset to Amazon S3 for Athena queries and model training. The process must run every night with minimal infrastructure administration.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create an Amazon EMR Spark application that reads the S3 files and JDBC tables, joins on the shared keys, removes duplicates, and writes Parquet to Amazon S3.
Create a SageMaker Processing job with custom pandas code that reads the S3 files and JDBC tables, joins on the shared keys, removes duplicates, and writes Parquet to Amazon S3.
Create a SageMaker Data Wrangler flow that imports the S3 files and JDBC tables, joins on the shared keys, removes duplicates, and exports a notebook.
Create an AWS Glue Studio ETL job that reads the S3 files and JDBC tables, joins on the shared keys, removes duplicates, and writes Parquet to Amazon S3.

correctText: Create an AWS Glue Studio ETL job that reads the S3 files and JDBC tables, joins on the shared keys, removes duplicates, and writes Parquet to Amazon S3.
questions.explanationHtml:
The most direct fit is AWS Glue Studio, because the requirement is a repeatable ETL pipeline that combines multiple data sources, transforms the data, and writes curated results to Amazon S3. Glue is designed for extract, transform, and load work, and Glue Studio provides a visual job editor for building data flows that include sources, joins, transformations, and targets.

The core tradeoff is not whether Spark can do the join. Spark can absolutely merge large datasets, and Amazon EMR is a strong choice when a team needs direct control over a distributed processing environment. In this case, however, the team asked for minimal infrastructure administration, so a managed Glue ETL job is a better operational match than managing EMR capacity or packaging custom processing code.

Data Wrangler is more naturally an interactive SageMaker data preparation tool for ML practitioners. It is valuable for exploring data, applying transformations, and generating code, but a shared nightly ETL job that reads from S3 and a JDBC source is better aligned with Glue. AWS documents Glue Studio join capabilities in Joining datasets, Glue source connectivity in Connecting to data, and Spark on EMR in Apache Spark on Amazon EMR.

questions.promptHtml: An industrial robotics manufacturer's ML telemetry team is preparing streaming features from robot sensor events. New controllers can publish events by using AWS service APIs, and the team must be able to reprocess recent events when preprocessing logic changes. A separate factory line already emits events by using Apache Kafka clients. The team wants to run custom Python or Scala stream-processing code over both feeds before writing prepared data to downstream storage. Which TWO actions should the team take?
questions.promptText:
An industrial robotics manufacturer's ML telemetry team is preparing streaming features from robot sensor events. New controllers can publish events by using AWS service APIs, and the team must be able to reprocess recent events when preprocessing logic changes. A separate factory line already emits events by using Apache Kafka clients. The team wants to run custom Python or Scala stream-processing code over both feeds before writing prepared data to downstream storage.

Which TWO actions should the team take?

options.text: Create Amazon Kinesis Data Streams for AWS-native events and Amazon MSK for the existing Kafka events.
Use Amazon Data Firehose for both feeds to deliver records directly to Amazon S3 without a replayable stream broker.
Use Amazon Athena after landing the prepared records in Amazon S3 to run ad hoc SQL analysis.
Use AWS Glue Studio to build a batch ETL workflow over files that have already landed in Amazon S3.
Run an Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink application to process the streams with custom code.

correctText: Create Amazon Kinesis Data Streams for AWS-native events and Amazon MSK for the existing Kafka events.
Run an Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink application to process the streams with custom code.
questions.explanationHtml:
Streaming ingestion services serve different roles. Amazon Kinesis Data Streams is designed for real-time collection and storage of records, with producer and consumer applications and the ability to replay data within the configured retention window. This fits an AWS-native event feed when downstream preprocessing might need to be rerun after a code change. See the Amazon Kinesis Data Streams overview and Kinesis Data Streams stream-management concepts.

Amazon MSK is the managed AWS service for Apache Kafka, so it is the natural fit when existing systems already produce and consume Kafka topics. Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink is then used for the processing layer, not as the durable event broker itself. It can run custom stream-processing applications and use streaming sources such as Kinesis Data Streams and Kafka topics from Amazon MSK, as described in Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink streaming sources and the Amazon MSK overview.

Amazon Data Firehose is often the right choice when the goal is serverless, near real-time delivery into destinations such as Amazon S3, with optional transformation and format conversion. It is not the right primary stream when the workload needs replay by consumers. Athena and AWS Glue Studio can be valuable after data has landed or when building ETL jobs, but they do not replace a replayable streaming ingestion service paired with a custom Flink processing application.

questions.domain: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.promptHtml: An environmental consulting firm's geospatial ML team runs intermittent Amazon SageMaker experiments and supporting data stores in a single AWS account. The engineering director wants periodic, high-level recommendations that can highlight cost optimization opportunities and operational risks such as resource limits, resiliency gaps, and security findings. The team has a Business Support plan and does not want to deploy monitoring agents or build custom reports from billing exports. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
An environmental consulting firm's geospatial ML team runs intermittent Amazon SageMaker experiments and supporting data stores in a single AWS account. The engineering director wants periodic, high-level recommendations that can highlight cost optimization opportunities and operational risks such as resource limits, resiliency gaps, and security findings. The team has a Business Support plan and does not want to deploy monitoring agents or build custom reports from billing exports.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use AWS Cost and Usage Reports to export detailed billing data to Amazon S3 for analysis.
Use AWS Budgets to create cost and usage budgets with notifications and actions.
Use AWS Cost Explorer to build cost and usage reports and forecast upcoming spend.
Use AWS Trusted Advisor to review account recommendations in the relevant check categories.

correctText: Use AWS Trusted Advisor to review account recommendations in the relevant check categories.
questions.explanationHtml:
AWS Trusted Advisor is the best fit when the requirement is a high-level account assessment rather than a custom cost analytics workflow. Trusted Advisor evaluates an AWS account and provides recommendations in operational categories such as cost optimization, security, performance, fault tolerance, service limits, and operational excellence, as described in AWS Trusted Advisor Recommendations.

Cost Explorer, AWS Budgets, and Cost and Usage Reports are cost management tools, but they solve different problems. Cost Explorer helps teams analyze historical cost and usage and forecast spending, as covered in AWS Cost Explorer overview. AWS Budgets is designed for threshold-based tracking and alerts, as described in AWS Budgets documentation, while Cost and Usage Reports deliver detailed billing data to Amazon S3 for later analysis, as described in AWS Cost and Usage Reports documentation.

The practical distinction is that cost analysis tools help answer where money is going or when spending crosses a threshold. Trusted Advisor helps answer what AWS account-level improvements should be considered, including cost and operational risk recommendations, with less setup effort for this scenario.

questions.promptHtml: A digital publishing platform's content intelligence team is preparing reviewer annotations for an ML model that predicts article policy violations. The data arrives from several internal web applications, and each annotation can include different nested attributes depending on the review workflow. Engineers need to inspect raw records during quality checks, and the data is used mainly as an interchange format before preprocessing rather than for large analytical scans of selected columns. Which data format should the team use for the raw annotation files?
questions.promptText:
A digital publishing platform's content intelligence team is preparing reviewer annotations for an ML model that predicts article policy violations. The data arrives from several internal web applications, and each annotation can include different nested attributes depending on the review workflow. Engineers need to inspect raw records during quality checks, and the data is used mainly as an interchange format before preprocessing rather than for large analytical scans of selected columns.

Which data format should the team use for the raw annotation files?

options.text: Store the annotation records as Parquet files in Amazon S3.
Store the annotation records as ORC files in Amazon S3.
Store the annotation records as CSV files in Amazon S3.
Store the annotation records as JSON files in Amazon S3.

correctText: Store the annotation records as JSON files in Amazon S3.
questions.explanationHtml:
JSON is a strong fit when raw ML preparation data is semi-structured, has variable fields, and needs to remain easy for engineers or analysts to inspect. It represents data as key-value structures and can naturally express nested objects, which makes it practical for annotation payloads that differ by workflow.

Parquet and ORC solve a different problem. They are columnar formats, so they are most useful when analytics engines query large datasets and read only some columns, reducing unnecessary I/O. AWS guidance for Athena discusses this tradeoff in Amazon Athena guidance on columnar storage formats, and Redshift Spectrum documentation similarly describes columnar format benefits in Amazon Redshift Spectrum data files.

CSV is useful for small, flat, tabular data that must be exchanged with spreadsheet tools, but it is a poor match for records with nested and inconsistent attributes. AWS Glue supports many file formats for ETL, including CSV, JSON, Parquet, and ORC, as shown in AWS Glue ETL input and output formats, so the decision should be driven by the data shape and access pattern rather than support alone.

questions.domain: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.promptHtml: A regional grocery chain's demand forecasting team uses AWS Step Functions to orchestrate nightly AWS Glue ETL jobs and an Amazon SageMaker batch transform job. Some runs complete late because an ETL state fails or a job errors before forecasts are produced. The team needs an AWS managed way to alert operators about these runtime failures and to inspect logs for troubleshooting, without writing a custom polling service. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A regional grocery chain's demand forecasting team uses AWS Step Functions to orchestrate nightly AWS Glue ETL jobs and an Amazon SageMaker batch transform job. Some runs complete late because an ETL state fails or a job errors before forecasts are produced. The team needs an AWS managed way to alert operators about these runtime failures and to inspect logs for troubleshooting, without writing a custom polling service.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Schedule Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor jobs for the batch transform output, publish constraint violations to CloudWatch, and notify responders through Amazon SNS.
Enable AWS CloudTrail Insights for the account, route insight events through Amazon EventBridge, and notify responders through Amazon SNS.
Configure AWS Config rules for the workflow resources, route compliance changes through Amazon EventBridge, and notify responders through Amazon SNS.
Create Amazon CloudWatch alarms for AWS Step Functions and AWS Glue failure metrics, centralize job logs in CloudWatch Logs, and notify responders through Amazon SNS.

correctText: Create Amazon CloudWatch alarms for AWS Step Functions and AWS Glue failure metrics, centralize job logs in CloudWatch Logs, and notify responders through Amazon SNS.
questions.explanationHtml:
For operational failures in a data processing and inference workflow, use Amazon CloudWatch at the workflow and job layers. AWS Step Functions emits execution metrics that can be used to alarm on failed workflows, while AWS Glue observability and logs help identify ETL job errors and performance bottlenecks. See AWS Step Functions CloudWatch metrics and AWS Glue Observability metrics.

The important distinction is between runtime health and model behavior. Runtime health asks whether the workflow, ETL job, or inference job completed successfully and whether operators can inspect logs. Model behavior asks whether the data, predictions, or quality metrics have drifted, which is where Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor is more appropriate.

CloudTrail Insights and AWS Config are valuable governance tools, but they answer different questions. CloudTrail helps audit API activity and detect unusual management event patterns, while Config tracks resource configuration and compliance state. Neither is the primary managed mechanism for alerting on failed Step Functions executions and failed Glue processing jobs.

questions.domain: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.promptHtml: A maritime logistics firm's risk modeling team trains a distributed deep learning model in Amazon SageMaker AI on multiple instances. The team already encrypts S3 training data and model artifacts with AWS KMS. A new compliance control requires encryption for the traffic that the training containers exchange with each other during training. Which action should the ML engineer take?
questions.promptText:
A maritime logistics firm's risk modeling team trains a distributed deep learning model in Amazon SageMaker AI on multiple instances. The team already encrypts S3 training data and model artifacts with AWS KMS. A new compliance control requires encryption for the traffic that the training containers exchange with each other during training.

Which action should the ML engineer take?

options.text: Configure SSE-KMS on the S3 bucket that stores the training artifacts.
Launch the training job in a private VPC with an S3 VPC endpoint.
Enable inter-container traffic encryption for the SageMaker AI training job.
Use CloudTrail to log SageMaker AI API activity to Amazon S3.

correctText: Enable inter-container traffic encryption for the SageMaker AI training job.
questions.explanationHtml:
For distributed training in Amazon SageMaker AI, encryption at rest and encryption in transit are separate controls. Using AWS KMS for S3 training data and model artifacts protects stored data, but it does not automatically cover the traffic exchanged between training containers while the job is running.

The SageMaker AI control that matches this requirement is inter-container traffic encryption, also called inter-node training communication encryption in many training contexts. This setting is enabled when configuring a training or tuning job and is intended for workloads that must protect communication between training nodes, with the practical tradeoff that it can add overhead for some deep learning jobs.

A private VPC and an S3 VPC endpoint are valuable for network isolation and private access to data sources, but they solve a different problem. CloudTrail is also important for governance and auditing because it records SageMaker AI API activity, but logging who did what is not the same as encrypting training traffic.

For more information, see Encryption in transit for SageMaker AI, Encryption at rest for SageMaker AI, and Logging SageMaker AI API calls with AWS CloudTrail.

questions.promptHtml: A dental insurance administrator's actuarial ML team has historical tabular claims data in Amazon S3 and a numeric label for final claim cost. The team expects non-linear interactions among procedure, provider, and patient features. The team wants to use a managed SageMaker training option and avoid maintaining a custom training container. Which approach best matches these modeling requirements?
questions.promptText:
A dental insurance administrator's actuarial ML team has historical tabular claims data in Amazon S3 and a numeric label for final claim cost. The team expects non-linear interactions among procedure, provider, and patient features. The team wants to use a managed SageMaker training option and avoid maintaining a custom training container.

Which approach best matches these modeling requirements?

options.text: Create an Amazon Bedrock agent that invokes a Lambda function to score each claim record.
Train a SageMaker built-in Linear Learner model after converting claim costs into cost bands.
Train a SageMaker built-in XGBoost model for regression by using the claims data from Amazon S3.
Deploy a SageMaker JumpStart text generation foundation model and prompt it with claim records.

correctText: Train a SageMaker built-in XGBoost model for regression by using the claims data from Amazon S3.
questions.explanationHtml:
For a tabular supervised learning problem with a numeric target, the first decision is whether the task is a conventional ML problem or a generative AI problem. Here the target is final claim cost, so the model development task is regression, not text generation, document summarization, or conversational reasoning.

SageMaker built-in algorithms are intended for common ML tasks where you want managed training without packaging your own algorithm container. XGBoost is a strong fit when the data is tabular and the relationships are expected to be non-linear, because boosted decision trees can capture feature interactions that a simple linear model might miss. AWS documents the built-in algorithm choices on Use Amazon SageMaker built-in algorithms or pretrained models.

SageMaker JumpStart and Amazon Bedrock are important choices for pretrained models, foundation models, examples, and solution accelerators. They are not automatically the best answer for every ML task. When the requirement is a managed supervised training job for tabular regression, selecting a foundation model or agent framework would usually add operational and modeling complexity rather than reduce it. For context, see SageMaker JumpStart and Using Amazon Bedrock foundation models.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: A tax preparation software vendor's ML platform team hosts a document classification model on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. The application servers that call the endpoint run in private subnets that do not have NAT gateway access. The inference container does not need to reach private databases or internal APIs, and security policy requires inference invocations to stay on the AWS private network. Which action should the team take to meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A tax preparation software vendor's ML platform team hosts a document classification model on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. The application servers that call the endpoint run in private subnets that do not have NAT gateway access. The inference container does not need to reach private databases or internal APIs, and security policy requires inference invocations to stay on the AWS private network.

Which action should the team take to meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a gateway VPC endpoint for Amazon S3 in the VPC and allow HTTPS from the application security group.
Create an interface VPC endpoint for SageMaker Runtime in the VPC and allow HTTPS from the application security group.
Enable network isolation on the SageMaker model container and redeploy the endpoint with the existing application subnets.
Configure VpcConfig on the SageMaker model with the private subnets and allow HTTPS from the application security group.

correctText: Create an interface VPC endpoint for SageMaker Runtime in the VPC and allow HTTPS from the application security group.
questions.explanationHtml:
For SageMaker inference, separate the client invocation path from the model container network path. The application calls the SageMaker Runtime service to invoke a real-time endpoint, so private applications in subnets without NAT need an interface VPC endpoint for SageMaker Runtime. With private DNS and appropriate security group rules, those calls resolve to private IP addresses in the VPC instead of requiring public internet connectivity.

VpcConfig is a different control. It attaches the hosted model container to subnets and security groups so the container can access VPC resources, such as private feature services, databases, or other internal dependencies. In this scenario, the container does not need that access, so configuring VpcConfig would not address the private calling path from the application servers.

An Amazon S3 VPC endpoint is commonly needed when SageMaker jobs or containers must reach S3 privately, especially in tightly controlled VPC designs. However, S3 connectivity is not the same as invoking a SageMaker endpoint. Network isolation is also a separate feature, it restricts container network access and is not a substitute for a private SageMaker Runtime endpoint.

See the AWS documentation for Invoking SageMaker AI API and SageMaker Runtime privately from a VPC using AWS PrivateLink, SageMaker AI hosted endpoints VPC access, and the SageMaker VpcConfig API reference.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: A biopharmaceutical research lab's ML data engineering team receives batches of sequencing metadata as objects in an Amazon S3 landing bucket throughout the day. Existing AWS Glue jobs validate, transform, and catalog the data before model-training pipelines consume the curated output. The team wants ingestion to start automatically after uploads, avoid custom polling code, and use managed orchestration for the ETL steps. Which TWO actions should the team take to meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)
questions.promptText:
A biopharmaceutical research lab's ML data engineering team receives batches of sequencing metadata as objects in an Amazon S3 landing bucket throughout the day. Existing AWS Glue jobs validate, transform, and catalog the data before model-training pipelines consume the curated output. The team wants ingestion to start automatically after uploads, avoid custom polling code, and use managed orchestration for the ETL steps.

Which TWO actions should the team take to meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Configure the matched event rule to start an AWS Glue workflow that coordinates the existing ETL jobs after uploads arrive.
Run an Amazon ECS service on AWS Fargate that continuously polls the bucket and submits ETL jobs when objects appear.
Configure an AWS CodeBuild project in a CI pipeline to run ETL scripts when source code changes are committed.
Deploy an AWS Lambda function on a schedule to list the bucket and start ETL jobs for newly discovered objects.
Enable Amazon S3 event delivery to Amazon EventBridge for the landing bucket, and create a rule that matches object-created events.

correctText: Configure the matched event rule to start an AWS Glue workflow that coordinates the existing ETL jobs after uploads arrive.
Enable Amazon S3 event delivery to Amazon EventBridge for the landing bucket, and create a rule that matches object-created events.
questions.explanationHtml:
For event-driven ML data ingestion, the main design idea is to let the storage layer emit an event and let a managed orchestration service decide what happens next. Amazon S3 can send bucket events, such as object-created events, to Amazon EventBridge, where rules can match those events and route them to downstream targets. This avoids the common anti-pattern of writing pollers that repeatedly list a bucket to discover new files.

AWS Glue workflows provide managed orchestration for Glue ETL jobs, crawlers, and triggers, so they are a natural fit when the ingestion step is primarily a Glue-based data preparation pipeline. A rule can start the Glue workflow when upload events arrive, which keeps the process automated while preserving the existing ETL job structure. If the broader ML workflow later needs to coordinate additional services, teams can also use services such as AWS Step Functions or SageMaker Pipelines, but the core ingestion trigger remains the same event-driven pattern.

Lambda, ECS on Fargate, and CodeBuild are all useful services in the right context, but they do not provide the lowest-overhead fit here. Scheduled or continuous polling adds custom state management and wastes effort compared with managed object-event delivery. CodeBuild belongs in CI workflows, not as the primary mechanism for reacting to new training data in an ETL pipeline.

See the AWS documentation for using EventBridge with Amazon S3 events, enabling EventBridge event delivery for an S3 bucket, and AWS Glue workflows.

questions.promptHtml: A legal discovery software team's ML engineers are preparing JSON records from Amazon S3 to train a classical classifier that routes customer support tickets. Each record includes an issue_summary field that contains free-form text. The training algorithm requires fixed-length numeric feature vectors, and the team wants summaries that share many of the same words to have related feature representations. Which preprocessing step should the team apply?
questions.promptText:
A legal discovery software team's ML engineers are preparing JSON records from Amazon S3 to train a classical classifier that routes customer support tickets. Each record includes an issue_summary field that contains free-form text. The training algorithm requires fixed-length numeric feature vectors, and the team wants summaries that share many of the same words to have related feature representations.

Which preprocessing step should the team apply?

options.text: Tokenize the issue_summary text and convert the resulting terms into numeric feature vectors.
Apply one-hot encoding to each complete issue_summary value and use the columns as features.
Apply binary encoding to the Unicode characters in issue_summary and use the bits as features.
Apply label encoding to each complete issue_summary value and use the encoded value as a feature.

correctText: Tokenize the issue_summary text and convert the resulting terms into numeric feature vectors.
questions.explanationHtml:
For unstructured text, the useful preprocessing pattern is usually to turn text into units such as words, subwords, or terms, then convert those units into numbers. Tokenization is the first step in that process, and vectorization methods such as term counts, hashing, or TF-IDF can then produce fixed-length numeric features for a classifier.

The important mental model is that text models need a representation where related documents can share signal. If two support tickets both mention similar words, their feature vectors should reflect that similarity. Label encoding or one-hot encoding an entire summary treats each full text string as a separate category, so two nearly identical summaries can look completely unrelated to the model.

On AWS, this kind of preprocessing can be implemented in managed data preparation or processing workflows, such as Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler custom transformations or SageMaker Processing jobs. See Prepare ML Data with Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler and Process Data and Evaluate Models for AWS-managed options that support data preparation before training.

questions.promptHtml: An online mortgage brokerage's risk analytics team trains a tabular binary classification model in Amazon SageMaker to recommend loan application outcomes.
