The model has acceptable validation accuracy, but the compliance team needs a repeatable way to understand which applicant features contributed most to individual recommendations and to the model's overall behavior. The team wants to avoid building a custom feature attribution framework. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?
questions.promptText:
An online mortgage brokerage's risk analytics team trains a tabular binary classification model in Amazon SageMaker to recommend loan application outcomes. The model has acceptable validation accuracy, but the compliance team needs a repeatable way to understand which applicant features contributed most to individual recommendations and to the model's overall behavior. The team wants to avoid building a custom feature attribution framework.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST development effort?

options.text: Use SageMaker Experiments to compare training trials and choose the trial with the highest validation metric.
Query endpoint application logs with CloudWatch Logs Insights and count approval outcomes by feature values.
Run a SageMaker Clarify explainability analysis for the model and review the generated feature attribution results.
Create a SageMaker Model Monitor data quality baseline for the endpoint and review feature distribution drift.

correctText: Run a SageMaker Clarify explainability analysis for the model and review the generated feature attribution results.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker Clarify is the managed SageMaker capability used when an ML engineer needs to interpret model outputs and understand feature influence. For tabular models, Clarify can use SHAP-based feature attribution, which estimates how much each feature contributed to a prediction and can also summarize feature importance across a dataset.

This is different from monitoring whether production data has drifted. Model Monitor is useful for tracking changes in statistical properties, model quality, bias drift, and feature attribution drift after deployment, but a data quality baseline is not the same as explaining why a particular application was approved or denied.

SageMaker Experiments helps track model development work, such as training jobs, hyperparameters, metrics, and artifacts. It is valuable for comparing candidate models, but it is not the right tool for producing feature attribution explanations. CloudWatch Logs Insights can query logs, but log aggregation is not a substitute for an explainability method that is aware of the trained model and its predictions.

For more information, see Overview of SageMaker Clarify model explainability and SageMaker Clarify Shapley values.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: A live sports media platform's highlights team runs an ML model that analyzes uploaded video clips and returns tagging metadata. Individual requests can include large payloads and can take several minutes to process. Uploads arrive unpredictably during games, with long idle periods between events. The application must accept each request quickly, but users can receive results after processing is complete. The team wants to avoid paying for continuously running inference capacity when there is no traffic. Which deployment option best meets these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A live sports media platform's highlights team runs an ML model that analyzes uploaded video clips and returns tagging metadata. Individual requests can include large payloads and can take several minutes to process. Uploads arrive unpredictably during games, with long idle periods between events. The application must accept each request quickly, but users can receive results after processing is complete. The team wants to avoid paying for continuously running inference capacity when there is no traffic.

Which deployment option best meets these requirements?

options.text: Run Amazon SageMaker Batch Transform jobs for accumulated video clips.
Deploy the model to an Amazon SageMaker Serverless Inference endpoint.
Deploy the model to an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint with autoscaling.
Deploy the model to an Amazon SageMaker Asynchronous Inference endpoint.

correctText: Deploy the model to an Amazon SageMaker Asynchronous Inference endpoint.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon SageMaker Asynchronous Inference is designed for workloads where the request can be accepted quickly, queued, processed later, and written to an output location after inference completes. That makes it a strong fit when payloads are large, processing takes longer than a typical low-latency request, and traffic has idle periods that make always-on capacity inefficient.

Real-time inference optimizes for immediate responses from a persistent endpoint, which is useful for interactive applications that need low latency for each request. Serverless Inference reduces infrastructure management and can scale to zero for idle workloads, but the key tradeoff is that it is still a direct invocation pattern and can have cold starts, so it is not the best match for large, long-running inference jobs. Batch Transform is the offline option for scoring an entire dataset, but it is less appropriate when the application must accept individual event-driven requests during live operations.

The mental model is to choose the inference mode from the required response pattern first, then optimize cost and capacity. Use real-time for immediate low-latency responses, serverless for intermittent direct inference that can tolerate cold starts, asynchronous inference for queued near-real-time work with larger or slower requests, and batch transform for offline dataset scoring. For more detail, see Amazon SageMaker AI inference cost optimization, Asynchronous Inference, Serverless Inference, Real-time inference, and Batch Transform.

questions.promptHtml: A city transit authority's predictive maintenance team prepares vehicle telemetry and maintenance notes for ML training. The raw data, intermediate datasets, and processed training files are stored in Amazon S3 and are processed by AWS Glue ETL jobs and Amazon SageMaker Processing jobs. Compliance requirements state that the data must be protected while stored and while moving between managed services, and the security team must be able to control and audit access to encryption keys. Which TWO actions should the ML engineer take to meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A city transit authority's predictive maintenance team prepares vehicle telemetry and maintenance notes for ML training. The raw data, intermediate datasets, and processed training files are stored in Amazon S3 and are processed by AWS Glue ETL jobs and Amazon SageMaker Processing jobs. Compliance requirements state that the data must be protected while stored and while moving between managed services, and the security team must be able to control and audit access to encryption keys.

Which TWO actions should the ML engineer take to meet these requirements?

options.text: Apply masking or hashing recipes to sensitive columns in AWS Glue DataBrew and skip storage encryption controls.
Use Amazon Macie classification findings to mark sensitive objects before creating feature datasets and model training files.
Run preparation workloads only in private subnets with PrivateLink and omit service-level encryption configuration.
Require encrypted transport for data movement by using HTTPS or TLS for S3 access, ETL connections, and service traffic.
Configure customer managed AWS KMS keys for S3 buckets, AWS Glue security settings, and SageMaker Processing outputs.

correctText: Require encrypted transport for data movement by using HTTPS or TLS for S3 access, ETL connections, and service traffic.
Configure customer managed AWS KMS keys for S3 buckets, AWS Glue security settings, and SageMaker Processing outputs.
questions.explanationHtml:
For ML data preparation, separate the problem into data at rest and data in transit. AWS KMS provides managed cryptographic keys that AWS services can use for server-side encryption, while IAM and CloudTrail help control and audit key use. Amazon S3, AWS Glue, and SageMaker can use KMS-based encryption for stored data and service artifacts, depending on the resource being configured.

The second control is encrypted transport. S3 supports HTTPS and TLS for data in motion, and AWS Glue documents encryption in transit for supported processing traffic. Network isolation with VPCs and PrivateLink is valuable, but it is not the same as encrypting stored objects or enforcing encrypted protocols. Similarly, Macie, masking, and hashing help with sensitive data discovery or obfuscation, but they do not satisfy a complete encryption requirement for raw data, intermediate files, outputs, and service traffic.

For more detail, see AWS KMS cryptography essentials, Amazon S3 encryption overview, AWS Glue encryption at rest, AWS Glue encryption in transit, and Amazon SageMaker AI encryption at rest.

questions.promptHtml: An arts grant foundation's ML team is preparing a training dataset in Amazon S3 for a binary classifier that predicts whether an application should be shortlisted. The dataset is stored as tabular records that include numeric budget fields, essay text fields, and image-derived portfolio tags. Before training, the team must check whether shortlisted labels occur at different rates for two values of the applicant_residence facet. The team does not need to check whether the two facet values have different numbers of records. Which action will meet this requirement?
questions.promptText:
An arts grant foundation's ML team is preparing a training dataset in Amazon S3 for a binary classifier that predicts whether an application should be shortlisted. The dataset is stored as tabular records that include numeric budget fields, essay text fields, and image-derived portfolio tags. Before training, the team must check whether shortlisted labels occur at different rates for two values of the applicant_residence facet. The team does not need to check whether the two facet values have different numbers of records.

Which action will meet this requirement?

options.text: Run a SageMaker Model Monitor model quality baseline with Ground Truth labels after the endpoint is deployed.
Run a SageMaker Clarify pre-training bias analysis with the DPL method for the applicant_residence facet and the shortlisted label.
Run a SageMaker Data Wrangler Quick Model analysis to rank feature importance for the applicant_residence feature.
Run a SageMaker Clarify pre-training bias analysis with the CI method for the applicant_residence facet and the shortlisted label.

correctText: Run a SageMaker Clarify pre-training bias analysis with the DPL method for the applicant_residence facet and the shortlisted label.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker Clarify can measure bias in raw training data before model training, which is useful when a team wants to detect representational or outcome-related issues before those issues are learned by a model. In this scenario, the key question is whether the positive label, shortlisted, occurs at different rates for values of the applicant_residence facet. That is the role of Difference in Proportions of Labels, or DPL, which compares positive-label proportions across facet values.

Class Imbalance, or CI, answers a different question: whether one facet value has fewer records than another. CI can be important when a demographic group or other facet is underrepresented, but it does not directly measure whether positive outcomes are distributed differently. Data Wrangler Quick Model and SageMaker Model Monitor can be useful in the ML lifecycle, but they do not replace a Clarify pre-training bias analysis for this label-proportion requirement.

The Clarify documentation lists pre-training bias metrics such as CI and DPL in Measure pretraining bias. AWS also provides separate metric pages for Difference in Proportions of Labels and Class Imbalance. For the broader workflow, see Detect pretraining data bias and the Clarify tabular data notes in Tabular datasets.

questions.promptHtml: A renewable energy cooperative's grid analytics team is developing a solar output forecasting model in Amazon SageMaker. Engineers currently run notebooks manually, change feature processing code between trials, and save model artifacts to different Amazon S3 prefixes. The team needs another engineer to be able to rerun the same model development sequence later and identify which inputs and outputs were associated with each run. Which TWO actions should the team take? (Select TWO.)
questions.promptText:
A renewable energy cooperative's grid analytics team is developing a solar output forecasting model in Amazon SageMaker. Engineers currently run notebooks manually, change feature processing code between trials, and save model artifacts to different Amazon S3 prefixes. The team needs another engineer to be able to rerun the same model development sequence later and identify which inputs and outputs were associated with each run.

Which TWO actions should the team take? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Register every trial in SageMaker Model Registry as an approved production model version.
Overwrite a single Amazon S3 model artifact key after each successful validation run.
Define a SageMaker Pipelines workflow for feature processing, model training, and evaluation steps.
Use SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking to record workflow inputs, outputs, and artifacts.
Query training container logs with CloudWatch Logs Insights to infer run configuration history.

correctText: Define a SageMaker Pipelines workflow for feature processing, model training, and evaluation steps.
Use SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking to record workflow inputs, outputs, and artifacts.
questions.explanationHtml:
Reproducible model development depends on two complementary ideas: make the workflow repeatable, and make the relationships among assets traceable. Amazon SageMaker Pipelines addresses the first need by defining managed ML workflow steps such as processing, training, and evaluation so the same sequence can be run again consistently.

SageMaker ML Lineage Tracking addresses the second need by helping track the inputs, outputs, and artifacts that are associated with workflow steps. This gives engineers and auditors a clearer path from source data and processing jobs to the trained model artifact that was produced.

SageMaker Model Registry is valuable for cataloging trained model packages and managing model versions, but it is not a substitute for workflow orchestration or full experiment lineage. Similarly, log queries and manually managed S3 paths can help with troubleshooting, but they are weak foundations for repeatable experiments because they do not reliably preserve the executable workflow and asset graph.

questions.promptHtml: A specialty coffee retailer's demand science team prepares weekly store-level sales data from CSV files in Amazon S3 for a regression model. The raw feed often contains duplicate store-week records, missing inventory counts, and extreme promotion values. The team wants a visual workflow to profile data quality issues, apply repeatable cleaning and feature transforms, and get rapid feedback about whether the prepared features are useful before running a full training pipeline. The team wants to minimize custom code. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A specialty coffee retailer's demand science team prepares weekly store-level sales data from CSV files in Amazon S3 for a regression model. The raw feed often contains duplicate store-week records, missing inventory counts, and extreme promotion values. The team wants a visual workflow to profile data quality issues, apply repeatable cleaning and feature transforms, and get rapid feedback about whether the prepared features are useful before running a full training pipeline. The team wants to minimize custom code.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use Amazon QuickSight ML Insights to detect anomalies, build dashboards, and use the dashboard outputs as the cleaned training dataset.
Use AWS Glue Data Quality to author completeness rules, publish rule scores, and launch the full SageMaker training job after each ruleset run.
Use Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler in SageMaker Canvas to generate a data quality report, apply cleaning transforms, and run Quick Model feedback.
Use Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor to create a baseline, detect drift, and use production monitoring reports to select cleaning steps.

correctText: Use Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler in SageMaker Canvas to generate a data quality report, apply cleaning transforms, and run Quick Model feedback.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler is designed for the kind of pre-modeling work described here: importing data, profiling it, visualizing issues, transforming features, and preparing the result for ML workflows. The Data Quality and Insights Report helps surface problems such as duplicate rows, anomalous samples, and other data quality concerns, while Data Wrangler transforms support common cleaning and feature engineering operations. Quick Model is useful at this stage because it gives fast feedback about whether the prepared features have predictive value, without requiring the team to commit to a full production training workflow.

AWS Glue Data Quality is valuable when the main requirement is to evaluate datasets with defined rules and track quality scores in data engineering pipelines. It does not replace an interactive ML preparation environment where engineers visually inspect feature behavior, apply many ML-oriented transformations, and quickly evaluate target prediction quality. QuickSight is strong for dashboards and analysis, but it is not the right primary tool for repeatable ETL and ML feature preparation. SageMaker Model Monitor becomes relevant after a model is deployed, when production inputs and predictions need to be monitored for drift or quality deviations.

For more information, see SageMaker Data Wrangler overview, Data Wrangler Data Insights and Quality Report, and Data Wrangler transform reference.

questions.promptHtml: A manufacturing automation team's ML engineer is training a binary classification model with the Amazon SageMaker Linear Learner algorithm. The training objective initially improves, then repeatedly jumps upward and fails to settle near a stable validation loss. The team wants to improve convergence without changing algorithms or increasing training infrastructure. Which action should the ML engineer take?
questions.promptText:
A manufacturing automation team's ML engineer is training a binary classification model with the Amazon SageMaker Linear Learner algorithm. The training objective initially improves, then repeatedly jumps upward and fails to settle near a stable validation loss. The team wants to improve convergence without changing algorithms or increasing training infrastructure.

Which action should the ML engineer take?

options.text: Disable feature normalization and increase L1 regularization before rerunning the training job.
Decrease the learning_rate and shuffle the training records before rerunning the training job.
Increase the number of epochs and preserve the current record order before rerunning the training job.
Increase the learning_rate and preserve the current record order before rerunning the training job.

correctText: Decrease the learning_rate and shuffle the training records before rerunning the training job.
questions.explanationHtml:
Convergence in models trained with stochastic gradient descent depends heavily on the size and quality of each update step. If the learning_rate is too large, the optimizer can overshoot good parameter values, which can make loss bounce around instead of settling. If the learning rate is too small, training can converge very slowly, but the symptom in this scenario is instability rather than slow but steady progress.

Amazon SageMaker Linear Learner uses stochastic gradient descent style optimization and expects training data preparation choices, such as shuffling and normalization, to support effective learning. Shuffling matters because each mini-batch should be a useful sample of the training distribution rather than a block of similarly ordered records. Normalization matters because features with very different numeric scales can distort gradient updates and make optimization less stable.

Adding more epochs or more infrastructure is a common anti-pattern when the underlying optimization settings are poor. More compute does not fix an update rule that is stepping past useful weights, and it can increase cost without improving model quality. For more background, see Training parameters, How Linear Learner works, and Linear Learner hyperparameters.

questions.promptHtml: A global airline's revenue management ML team trains an Amazon SageMaker model every night from several hundred GB of preprocessed tabular data stored in Amazon S3. The training code reads the data sequentially from large shard files and does not require shared POSIX file semantics. Recent runs spend excessive time staging data before training begins. The team wants to improve startup time with the least operational overhead and keep the source dataset in S3. Which solution should the team use?
questions.promptText:
A global airline's revenue management ML team trains an Amazon SageMaker model every night from several hundred GB of preprocessed tabular data stored in Amazon S3. The training code reads the data sequentially from large shard files and does not require shared POSIX file semantics. Recent runs spend excessive time staging data before training begins. The team wants to improve startup time with the least operational overhead and keep the source dataset in S3.

Which solution should the team use?

options.text: Configure the training channel to use Amazon S3 with SageMaker Fast File input mode.
Copy the training dataset to Amazon EFS and mount it in the training job.
Link the S3 dataset to Amazon FSx for Lustre and train from the file system.
Configure the training channel to use Amazon S3 with SageMaker File input mode.

correctText: Configure the training channel to use Amazon S3 with SageMaker Fast File input mode.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon SageMaker AI supports several ways to make training data available to a training job. File input mode copies objects from Amazon S3 to local storage before the training container reads them, which is simple but can add significant startup time for large datasets. Fast File input mode presents S3 data in a file-like way so training can start sooner, and it is especially appropriate when the algorithm reads large files sequentially.

File systems such as Amazon EFS and Amazon FSx for Lustre solve different storage problems. EFS is elastic shared NFS storage, useful when applications need shared file access, but it requires the data to be in the file system. FSx for Lustre is designed for high-performance ML and HPC workloads and integrates with S3, but it introduces a separate file system that is unnecessary when the main goal is to reduce S3 staging time for sequential training reads. For this scenario, keeping the data in S3 and changing the SageMaker input mode gives the best tradeoff between performance improvement and operational simplicity. See Access Training Data, Best Practices for Choosing Training Input Mode, What is Amazon Elastic File System?, and What is Amazon FSx for Lustre?.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: A museum digitization program's ML engineering team uses Amazon SageMaker Projects to manage preprocessing code, a Dockerfile, and deployment templates for a model deployment pipeline. An engineer must update the endpoint deployment logic for a new model version. The team requires code review before changes reach the default branch, and the CI/CD pipeline must use reviewed repository history. Which Git workflow should the engineer use?
questions.promptText:
A museum digitization program's ML engineering team uses Amazon SageMaker Projects to manage preprocessing code, a Dockerfile, and deployment templates for a model deployment pipeline. An engineer must update the endpoint deployment logic for a new model version. The team requires code review before changes reach the default branch, and the CI/CD pipeline must use reviewed repository history.

Which Git workflow should the engineer use?

options.text: Create a feature branch, stage the changed files, run git pull, and wait for the CI/CD pipeline to detect the branch.
Create a feature branch, stage the changed files, commit the changes, and push the branch to the remote repository.
Create a feature branch, copy the changed files to Amazon S3, and configure the pipeline to load the latest files.
Edit the default branch locally, stage the changed files, commit the changes, and push directly to the remote repository.

correctText: Create a feature branch, stage the changed files, commit the changes, and push the branch to the remote repository.
questions.explanationHtml:
Git is used to manage source code as a sequence of versioned commits. In an ML operations workflow, that source code can include preprocessing scripts, training code, container definitions, pipeline definitions, and infrastructure templates. A feature branch lets an engineer work independently, while git add, git commit, and git push publish a reviewable, reproducible change set without immediately changing the default branch.

SageMaker Projects are designed to organize MLOps work with repositories and CI/CD workflows, so the repository should be the source of truth for code changes. Using Amazon S3 for model artifacts or datasets is common, but using an S3 object named as the latest version of deployment code bypasses the review and history model that Git provides. For basic Git command behavior, see Basic Git commands and What is AWS CodeCommit?. For how SageMaker Projects use repositories in MLOps workflows, see What are SageMaker Projects?.

questions.promptHtml: A multiplayer game studio's trust and safety team is evaluating a binary classification model that flags player accounts for bot activity. A false positive causes a legitimate player to be suspended, which is the highest business impact. The team wants to compare candidate models using a metric that focuses on how many flagged accounts are truly bots rather than on how many total bots are found. Which action should the ML engineer take to analyze model performance?
questions.promptText:
A multiplayer game studio's trust and safety team is evaluating a binary classification model that flags player accounts for bot activity. A false positive causes a legitimate player to be suspended, which is the highest business impact. The team wants to compare candidate models using a metric that focuses on how many flagged accounts are truly bots rather than on how many total bots are found.

Which action should the ML engineer take to analyze model performance?

options.text: Evaluate the candidate models by using recall from the confusion matrix.
Evaluate the candidate models by using RMSE on the prediction outputs.
Evaluate the candidate models by using precision from the confusion matrix.
Evaluate the candidate models by using overall accuracy on the validation set.

correctText: Evaluate the candidate models by using precision from the confusion matrix.
questions.explanationHtml:
For a binary classifier, the right metric depends on the operational cost of different error types. Precision answers the question, among the cases the model predicted as positive, how many were truly positive. In this scenario, that maps to how many flagged accounts were actually bots, so it is the best fit when false positives are the highest business impact.

Recall is the better metric when false negatives are more costly, such as when the team wants to find as many true bot accounts as possible even if some legitimate accounts are flagged. Accuracy can be misleading when classes are imbalanced, because it combines all correct predictions into one number. RMSE is a regression metric and is not the appropriate way to analyze a classification model's confusion matrix behavior.

Amazon SageMaker tools expose these model performance concepts in several places. SageMaker Autopilot describes classification metrics such as precision, recall, F1, accuracy, and AUC in Autopilot model candidate metrics, and its model insights documentation discusses confusion matrices and classification tradeoffs in Autopilot model insights.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: A telehealth provider's clinical documentation team hosts a deep learning model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. The current endpoint uses CPU instances and meets availability requirements, but latency is increasing during peak hours. The team wants to test the same model on GPU instances in production by sending a small percentage of live requests to the GPU-backed deployment, while most users continue to use the current CPU-backed deployment. The team must be able to adjust the traffic split without building a separate routing service. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A telehealth provider's clinical documentation team hosts a deep learning model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. The current endpoint uses CPU instances and meets availability requirements, but latency is increasing during peak hours. The team wants to test the same model on GPU instances in production by sending a small percentage of live requests to the GPU-backed deployment, while most users continue to use the current CPU-backed deployment. The team must be able to adjust the traffic split without building a separate routing service.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create separate batch transform jobs using CPU and GPU instance types, and compare the outputs after processing a sample dataset.
Create an endpoint configuration with two production variants, assign CPU and GPU instance types separately, and set variant weights for live traffic.
Create a separate real-time endpoint on GPU instances, and configure the application to route a small percentage of requests to it.
Create a SageMaker Processing job with GPU instances, and invoke the processing container from the application during peak traffic.

correctText: Create an endpoint configuration with two production variants, assign CPU and GPU instance types separately, and set variant weights for live traffic.
questions.explanationHtml:
For a SageMaker real-time endpoint, a production variant represents a hosted model configuration with its own compute resources, such as instance type and initial instance count. By placing the current CPU-backed deployment and the candidate GPU-backed deployment behind the same endpoint as separate variants, the team can use variant weights to control how much live traffic each variant receives.

This pattern is useful when the team needs to evaluate production behavior, such as latency, error rates, and model response characteristics, under real application traffic. It avoids building a custom router because SageMaker performs the traffic distribution at the endpoint level. The same concept can be used for A/B style tests of models, containers, or instance choices, as described in Test models in production.

The compute resources for hosted models are defined in endpoint configurations and production variants. The relevant resource model includes fields such as InstanceType, InitialInstanceCount, and traffic weighting, which are documented in CreateEndpointConfig and ProductionVariant. Batch transform and processing jobs are important SageMaker capabilities, but they are job-oriented rather than live traffic routing mechanisms.

questions.promptHtml: A marine conservation institute's analytics team uses AWS Glue Studio to transform raw ocean sensor readings in Amazon S3 into Parquet feature datasets for Amazon SageMaker. Some recent input batches contained null identifiers, duplicate observation records, and timestamps outside the expected range. The team needs the pipeline to validate these checks automatically during each ETL run before the transformed dataset is written. The team wants to minimize custom validation code. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A marine conservation institute's analytics team uses AWS Glue Studio to transform raw ocean sensor readings in Amazon S3 into Parquet feature datasets for Amazon SageMaker. Some recent input batches contained null identifiers, duplicate observation records, and timestamps outside the expected range. The team needs the pipeline to validate these checks automatically during each ETL run before the transformed dataset is written. The team wants to minimize custom validation code.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Run an AWS Glue DataBrew profile job after the AWS Glue ETL job writes the output dataset.
Use Amazon Macie to discover sensitive data in the S3 bucket before the ETL job runs.
Add a data quality ruleset to the AWS Glue ETL job and evaluate the rules before writing the output.
Create an Amazon Athena query dashboard that analysts review before starting SageMaker training.

correctText: Add a data quality ruleset to the AWS Glue ETL job and evaluate the rules before writing the output.
questions.explanationHtml:
AWS Glue Data Quality is a good fit when data validation must be part of a managed ETL workflow. In this scenario, the team already uses AWS Glue Studio to transform data, so adding rule evaluation in the job lets the pipeline check the data before writing the feature output. Rules can express common quality expectations such as required fields, uniqueness, and allowed value ranges, which maps directly to the null identifiers, duplicate records, and invalid timestamps in the scenario.

AWS Glue DataBrew is also relevant to data quality because it supports profiling datasets and validating rules in profile jobs, but it is better suited here as a separate visual profiling and preparation workflow. Running validation only after the ETL job writes the result does not protect downstream training data as directly as evaluating quality during the ETL job. Athena can support ad hoc SQL validation, and Macie can support sensitive data discovery, but neither provides the same managed, in-pipeline quality gate for an AWS Glue ETL job.

For more information, see AWS Glue Data Quality overview, AWS Glue Studio tutorial for evaluating data quality in ETL jobs, and AWS Glue DataBrew data quality validation.

questions.promptHtml: A legal analytics startup's e-discovery ML team fine-tunes a PyTorch transformer model on Amazon SageMaker. The model has more than 1 billion parameters and is constrained by GPU memory on a single instance. The team launches training runs through SageMaker automatic model tuning, and the training script emits a validation loss metric after each epoch. Many tuning trials stop improving early but continue to run for all configured epochs. The team wants to reduce elapsed training time and compute usage without changing the model family or objective metric. Which TWO actions should the team take?
questions.promptText:
A legal analytics startup's e-discovery ML team fine-tunes a PyTorch transformer model on Amazon SageMaker. The model has more than 1 billion parameters and is constrained by GPU memory on a single instance. The team launches training runs through SageMaker automatic model tuning, and the training script emits a validation loss metric after each epoch. Many tuning trials stop improving early but continue to run for all configured epochs. The team wants to reduce elapsed training time and compute usage without changing the model family or objective metric.

Which TWO actions should the team take?

options.text: Configure SageMaker distributed model parallelism to partition the PyTorch model across GPUs.
Enable SageMaker Training Compiler together with SageMaker distributed training libraries.
Use SageMaker distributed data parallelism to split the model state across GPUs.
Change the tuning strategy to grid search across every candidate hyperparameter value.
Set early stopping to Auto for the SageMaker automatic model tuning job.

correctText: Configure SageMaker distributed model parallelism to partition the PyTorch model across GPUs.
Set early stopping to Auto for the SageMaker automatic model tuning job.
questions.explanationHtml:
Two different bottlenecks appear in this scenario. The model is large enough that model memory is a constraint, and many tuning trials are wasting epochs after their validation loss has stopped improving. The right response is to address both: use SageMaker distributed model parallelism for the large PyTorch model, and enable early stopping for the automatic model tuning job.

SageMaker distributed training includes different patterns for different bottlenecks. Data parallelism is useful when the model can fit on each worker and the training data or gradient computation is the scaling problem. Model parallelism is for cases where the model itself needs to be partitioned across GPUs or instances, which matches a transformer with more than 1 billion parameters and GPU memory pressure. See the SageMaker distributed training overview in Distributed training with Amazon SageMaker.

Early stopping in SageMaker automatic model tuning is useful when training jobs report an objective metric over time, such as validation loss after each epoch. It can stop underperforming jobs before they complete every epoch, reducing billable training time and helping avoid unnecessary overfitting work. The behavior is described in Stop training jobs early.

The distractors miss the operational tradeoff. Grid search is a brute force tuning method and usually expands training work. Data parallelism is not the right mechanism for splitting a model that is too large for a single GPU. SageMaker Training Compiler can optimize supported deep learning jobs, but it is not the correct choice when the solution requires SageMaker distributed training libraries, as covered in SageMaker Training Compiler.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: A regional pharmacy chain's medication adherence team hosts a refill-risk model on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. Traffic is low overnight, increases sharply when pharmacies open each weekday morning, and then varies during the day when reminder campaigns run. The team must meet a strict latency target during the opening-hour surge and wants to avoid manual changes to endpoint capacity. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A regional pharmacy chain's medication adherence team hosts a refill-risk model on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. Traffic is low overnight, increases sharply when pharmacies open each weekday morning, and then varies during the day when reminder campaigns run. The team must meet a strict latency target during the opening-hour surge and wants to avoid manual changes to endpoint capacity.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Replace the real-time endpoint with batch transform jobs. Schedule jobs before opening and start more jobs when campaigns launch.
Register the endpoint variant as a scalable target. Add only scheduled actions for opening and closing, and leave instance count fixed between them.
Register the endpoint variant as a scalable target. Add a scheduled action before opening, and add target tracking on invocations per instance.
Register the endpoint variant as a scalable target. Add only target tracking on invocations per instance, and keep overnight minimum capacity low.

correctText: Register the endpoint variant as a scalable target. Add a scheduled action before opening, and add target tracking on invocations per instance.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker AI endpoint auto scaling uses Application Auto Scaling to adjust the desired instance count for an endpoint variant. For workloads with changing traffic, target tracking policies are commonly used to keep a utilization-style metric near a target value, such as invocations per instance. This gives the endpoint a feedback loop that adds or removes capacity as demand changes.

Predictable time-based demand is a different problem. If traffic reliably jumps at a known time, a scheduled action can adjust the scalable target's minimum and/or maximum capacity before the spike begins, helping ensure capacity bounds are appropriate before the endpoint becomes busy. Combining scheduled scaling with a demand-based policy is a practical pattern: scheduled scaling prepares for known demand, and target tracking handles the less predictable variation afterward.

Using only scheduled scaling is too rigid for campaign-driven bursts, and using only target tracking can be too reactive for a sharp known surge with strict latency requirements. Batch transform is a separate inference mode for processing datasets asynchronously, not a replacement for a real-time endpoint that must serve individual requests during business hours. For more information, see SageMaker AI endpoint auto scaling overview, Application Auto Scaling target tracking scaling policies, and Application Auto Scaling scheduled scaling.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: A public transportation agency's analytics team stores new monthly ridership data in Amazon S3. The team has an Amazon SageMaker Pipeline that preprocesses the data, trains a model, evaluates the model, and registers an approved model version. The team wants the workflow to start automatically when a new data file arrives, pass the new data location into the workflow, and alert the operations channel if the workflow or training job fails. The team wants to avoid custom polling code. Which TWO actions will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A public transportation agency's analytics team stores new monthly ridership data in Amazon S3. The team has an Amazon SageMaker Pipeline that preprocesses the data, trains a model, evaluates the model, and registers an approved model version. The team wants the workflow to start automatically when a new data file arrives, pass the new data location into the workflow, and alert the operations channel if the workflow or training job fails. The team wants to avoid custom polling code.

Which TWO actions will meet these requirements?

options.text: Run a SageMaker Batch Transform job on each uploaded file and register the transform output as the next model version.
Configure an AWS Lambda function on a schedule to list the S3 prefix and call CreateTrainingJob for each newly discovered object.
Configure an Amazon EventBridge rule for S3 object-created events to start the SageMaker Pipeline with the new object URI as a pipeline parameter.
Configure AWS CodePipeline to deploy the current approved model to production whenever the S3 prefix receives a new training file.
Configure Amazon EventBridge rules for SageMaker pipeline or training job failure state changes to publish alerts to an Amazon SNS topic.

correctText: Configure an Amazon EventBridge rule for S3 object-created events to start the SageMaker Pipeline with the new object URI as a pipeline parameter.
Configure Amazon EventBridge rules for SageMaker pipeline or training job failure state changes to publish alerts to an Amazon SNS topic.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker Pipelines is designed to represent an ML workflow as a repeatable directed set of steps, such as preprocessing, training, evaluation, model registration, and deployment. In this scenario, the team already has that workflow, so the best automation pattern is to start a pipeline execution when new data arrives and pass run-specific values, such as the S3 URI, as parameters. AWS documents this pattern in Define a pipeline and Schedule pipeline executions with Amazon EventBridge.

Amazon EventBridge is the managed event routing service that fits both sides of the requirement: triggering the workflow and reacting to failures. SageMaker emits state change events for resources such as training jobs and pipeline executions, which can be matched by EventBridge rules and routed to targets such as notification workflows. The relevant SageMaker event integration is described in Automating Amazon SageMaker with Amazon EventBridge.

Polling an S3 prefix with scheduled Lambda code is an avoidable operational burden and can create duplicate handling, missed edge cases, and extra code to maintain. Starting a single CreateTrainingJob call directly can be valid for simple training, but it does not use the existing pipeline stages unless the team rebuilds the orchestration logic itself. For reference, the low-level training job configuration is documented in CreateTrainingJob.

Batch Transform and direct production deployment solve different problems. Batch Transform performs offline inference over a dataset, while deploying an already approved model does not retrain or evaluate anything. SageMaker deployment options are useful after a model is selected, as covered in Deploy models for inference, but they do not replace the model-building pipeline in this scenario.

questions.promptHtml: An agricultural insurance cooperative's ML team is preparing tabular crop claim data in Amazon SageMaker Studio. The team has access to managed SageMaker data preparation and responsible AI capabilities. The target label is whether a claim was approved. The dataset includes region and inspection_channel columns, and the team suspects selection bias because one region has far fewer labeled examples after a late mobile app rollout. The team also suspects measurement bias because severity scores from phone inspections may not be consistent with severity scores from field inspections. The model has not been trained. The team must assess the raw training data for bias and prepare a less biased dataset before training, with managed SageMaker capabilities and minimal custom code. Which TWO actions should the team take?
questions.promptText:
An agricultural insurance cooperative's ML team is preparing tabular crop claim data in Amazon SageMaker Studio. The team has access to managed SageMaker data preparation and responsible AI capabilities. The target label is whether a claim was approved. The dataset includes region and inspection_channel columns, and the team suspects selection bias because one region has far fewer labeled examples after a late mobile app rollout. The team also suspects measurement bias because severity scores from phone inspections may not be consistent with severity scores from field inspections. The model has not been trained. The team must assess the raw training data for bias and prepare a less biased dataset before training, with managed SageMaker capabilities and minimal custom code.

Which TWO actions should the team take?

options.text: Use SageMaker Data Wrangler transformations to rebalance underrepresented facet values and standardize inconsistent feature values before exporting the training data.
Generate a SageMaker Clarify pre-training bias report in SageMaker Studio or Data Wrangler using the approval label and the suspected facet columns.
Use Amazon Macie to discover protected attributes in Amazon S3 and remove those columns before any bias or quality analysis.
Run SageMaker Clarify post-training bias analysis after training and use predicted labels to remove rows from the original dataset.
Configure SageMaker Model Monitor bias drift checks on a production endpoint and use live prediction alerts as the first fairness assessment.

correctText: Use SageMaker Data Wrangler transformations to rebalance underrepresented facet values and standardize inconsistent feature values before exporting the training data.
Generate a SageMaker Clarify pre-training bias report in SageMaker Studio or Data Wrangler using the approval label and the suspected facet columns.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker Clarify can measure bias in data before a model is trained. In a pre-training analysis, the team identifies a label, such as claim approval, and one or more facets, such as region or inspection_channel, then reviews whether representation or label outcomes differ across those facets. This workflow is appropriate because the scenario asks for raw-data bias assessment before training, using managed SageMaker capabilities with minimal custom code. AWS describes the pre-training bias workflow in Overview of pre-training data bias in Amazon SageMaker Clarify and raw-dataset metrics in Measure pre-training bias.

After bias is identified, mitigation is a data preparation activity, not only a monitoring activity. SageMaker Data Wrangler is appropriate because it provides a visual workflow for profiling, transforming, and exporting data, and it can be used in SageMaker Studio with minimal custom code. For selection bias, rebalancing underrepresented facet values can reduce the degree to which the model learns mostly from overrepresented groups. For measurement bias, standardizing or transforming inconsistent feature values helps make the same real-world concept mean the same thing across data collection channels. AWS describes Data Wrangler bias report generation in Create bias reports in Data Wrangler and preparation transformations in Transform data.

Post-deployment monitoring, post-training bias metrics, and privacy discovery can all be valuable in the larger ML lifecycle, but they solve different problems. Model Monitor is for deployed models, so it is not the first step when the model has not been trained. Post-training Clarify evaluates model outputs, while the scenario asks for raw-data assessment before training. Macie can help protect sensitive data, but simply removing protected attributes before measuring bias can hide the very evidence needed to detect unfair representation or label imbalance.

questions.promptHtml: A professional sports league's analytics engineering team receives nightly JSON event logs from stadium sensors in Amazon S3. The team must join the logs with venue reference data, remove unused fields, convert the result to Parquet, and expose the prepared dataset for Athena queries that feed ML feature exploration. The team wants a visual managed ETL workflow and does not want to operate an Amazon EMR cluster or run ad hoc notebooks for each load. Which TWO actions will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
A professional sports league's analytics engineering team receives nightly JSON event logs from stadium sensors in Amazon S3. The team must join the logs with venue reference data, remove unused fields, convert the result to Parquet, and expose the prepared dataset for Athena queries that feed ML feature exploration. The team wants a visual managed ETL workflow and does not want to operate an Amazon EMR cluster or run ad hoc notebooks for each load.

Which TWO actions will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Build a SageMaker Data Wrangler flow that exports a Jupyter notebook, and run the notebook manually for each nightly load.
Register the transformed S3 dataset in the AWS Glue Data Catalog so Athena can query the prepared tables for feature exploration.
Launch a long-running Amazon EMR cluster with Apache Spark, and submit PySpark jobs manually to transform each nightly load.
Create Amazon QuickSight analyses with calculated fields, and use the dashboards as the primary transformation layer for the logs.
Create an AWS Glue Studio visual ETL job that reads the S3 logs, joins the reference data, applies field transforms, and writes Parquet output to S3.

correctText: Register the transformed S3 dataset in the AWS Glue Data Catalog so Athena can query the prepared tables for feature exploration.
Create an AWS Glue Studio visual ETL job that reads the S3 logs, joins the reference data, applies field transforms, and writes Parquet output to S3.
questions.explanationHtml:
AWS Glue Studio is the best fit when the main task is managed ETL: read data from Amazon S3, visually define joins and transformations, and write prepared data back to S3 in an analytics-friendly format such as Parquet. The visual job model reduces operational overhead compared with running a self-managed Spark environment, while still using a scalable ETL service designed for this type of transformation work. The AWS Glue Studio documentation describes managed transform nodes and visual ETL job construction in AWS Glue Studio managed transform nodes.

For ML feature exploration, the transformed data should also be discoverable by query engines. Registering the output in the AWS Glue Data Catalog gives Athena the metadata it needs to query data that remains in Amazon S3, which fits a data lake pattern for prepared datasets. SageMaker Data Wrangler is valuable for interactive ML data preparation, but an exported notebook that someone manually runs every night is not the lowest-overhead production ETL pattern, as described in SageMaker Data Wrangler transform data. Amazon EMR with Spark is powerful for distributed processing, as covered in Apache Spark on Amazon EMR, but the scenario explicitly prefers avoiding cluster operations. QuickSight should remain a visualization and analysis tool, not the primary transformation system for raw data pipelines.

questions.promptHtml: An industrial IoT equipment maker's predictive maintenance team trains a neural network on Amazon SageMaker by using a fixed sensor dataset. Each run uses the same number of epochs. Training logs show significant overhead from many small optimization updates, and GPU memory utilization is consistently low. The team wants to shorten training runs while keeping the same number of full passes over the dataset and avoiding additional instances. Which action should the team take?
questions.promptText:
An industrial IoT equipment maker's predictive maintenance team trains a neural network on Amazon SageMaker by using a fixed sensor dataset. Each run uses the same number of epochs. Training logs show significant overhead from many small optimization updates, and GPU memory utilization is consistently low. The team wants to shorten training runs while keeping the same number of full passes over the dataset and avoiding additional instances.

Which action should the team take?

options.text: Increase the epochs value and keep the mini_batch_size unchanged.
Decrease the mini_batch_size value and keep the epoch count unchanged.
Decrease the learning_rate value and keep the epoch count unchanged.
Increase the mini_batch_size value and keep the epoch count unchanged.

correctText: Increase the mini_batch_size value and keep the epoch count unchanged.
questions.explanationHtml:
In iterative training, an epoch is a complete pass over the training dataset, while a step or iteration commonly corresponds to processing one batch and applying an optimization update. If the dataset size and epoch count stay the same, increasing mini_batch_size generally reduces the number of steps per epoch because each step consumes more examples.

This is a practical performance tradeoff, not a free accuracy guarantee. Larger batches can use GPU memory more efficiently and reduce per-step overhead, but they can also change optimization behavior, so the team should compare validation metrics after the change. Increasing epochs would process the data more times, decreasing batch size would create even more steps, and changing learning rate affects update magnitude rather than the amount of work per epoch. For related SageMaker terminology, see Distributed training in Amazon SageMaker and the SageMaker Linear Learner hyperparameter descriptions for epochs, learning_rate, and mini_batch_size.

questions.promptHtml: A specialty grocery retailer's loyalty analytics team wants to predict which shoppers will respond to a new subscription delivery offer. The team has several years of point-of-sale history, but only one small pilot campaign contains explicit response labels for this offer. A simple SQL segmentation rule based on purchase frequency already meets the marketing team's minimum lift target for a similar offer. The team wants to decide whether to invest in a custom ML model before building a full training pipeline. Which action should the ML engineer take FIRST?
questions.promptText:
A specialty grocery retailer's loyalty analytics team wants to predict which shoppers will respond to a new subscription delivery offer. The team has several years of point-of-sale history, but only one small pilot campaign contains explicit response labels for this offer. A simple SQL segmentation rule based on purchase frequency already meets the marketing team's minimum lift target for a similar offer. The team wants to decide whether to invest in a custom ML model before building a full training pipeline.

Which action should the ML engineer take FIRST?

options.text: Train a deep learning model with every shopper attribute and tune many hyperparameters by using random search.
Run a SageMaker Autopilot HPO job on all purchase history and deploy the top leaderboard model for the offer.
Load the raw campaign files into an Amazon S3 data lake and defer target selection until pipeline automation is complete.
Define the target and success metric, profile the labeled pilot data, and compare a small prototype against the current rule.

correctText: Define the target and success metric, profile the labeled pilot data, and compare a small prototype against the current rule.
questions.explanationHtml:
Before investing in a custom model, an ML engineer should verify that the business goal can be expressed as a supervised learning problem with a clear target variable, meaningful evaluation metric, and enough relevant labeled examples. In this scenario, years of transaction history may be useful features, but the response labels for this specific offer exist only in a small pilot, so the labeled data is the limiting factor.

A simple baseline matters because ML should improve on an existing process enough to justify its extra cost and operational complexity. If a SQL rule already meets the business threshold, a prototype model should be compared against that rule before the team commits to SageMaker Pipelines, large-scale training, or deployment automation.

Automated ML tools such as SageMaker Autopilot can help after the problem is framed, but they do not remove the need to define the target, validate the data, and evaluate whether ML is the right approach. Similarly, choosing deep learning and broad hyperparameter tuning too early is an anti-pattern when the complexity of the problem and the value over a simpler solution have not been established.

AWS Well-Architected guidance emphasizes framing the ML problem, checking data availability, and considering simpler alternatives before building a custom solution. For more context, see ML problem framing, Determine if machine learning is the right solution, and Data collection.

questions.domain: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.promptHtml: An online education platform's ML operations team runs Amazon SageMaker training jobs, processing jobs, and endpoints for several product teams in one AWS account. Finance wants monthly alerts and cost analysis by product team and lifecycle stage, such as training, inference, and experimentation. The team wants to prepare the infrastructure so that future workloads can be attributed consistently with minimal manual reconciliation. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
An online education platform's ML operations team runs Amazon SageMaker training jobs, processing jobs, and endpoints for several product teams in one AWS account. Finance wants monthly alerts and cost analysis by product team and lifecycle stage, such as training, inference, and experimentation. The team wants to prepare the infrastructure so that future workloads can be attributed consistently with minimal manual reconciliation.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Enable CloudTrail for SageMaker API activity, deliver trails to Amazon S3, and query CreateTrainingJob and CreateEndpoint events in Athena for chargeback.
Create CloudWatch dashboards for SageMaker endpoint invocations and latency, add alarms for utilization spikes, and review the dashboards with finance at month end.

Define required user-defined tags such as ProductTeam and MLStage, apply them to SageMaker resources, activate the tag keys for cost allocation, and create AWS Budgets and Cost Explorer views filtered by those tags.
Register every model version in SageMaker Model Registry, add approval metadata for each product team, and summarize approved model packages for finance.

correctText: Define required user-defined tags such as ProductTeam and MLStage, apply them to SageMaker resources, activate the tag keys for cost allocation, and create AWS Budgets and Cost Explorer views filtered by those tags.
questions.explanationHtml:
For ML cost monitoring, the practical starting point is a consistent tagging strategy. Tags such as ProductTeam, MLStage, Environment, or Project let teams attach business context to resources so that finance and engineering can analyze spend without manually reconstructing which workload created each charge.

AWS cost tools can use tags only as useful reporting dimensions when the tagging approach is standardized and the relevant tag keys are enabled for cost allocation. AWS explains how activated tags organize costs in billing reports in Using cost allocation tags, and provides guidance for user-defined tags in User-defined cost allocation tags. After the tags are available for billing, teams can use AWS Budgets for alerts and AWS Cost Explorer for analysis, including filtering by tags as described in Filtering the data that you want to view.

CloudWatch, CloudTrail, and SageMaker Model Registry remain important, but they solve different problems. CloudWatch monitors runtime behavior and alarms on metrics, CloudTrail audits API calls, and Model Registry manages model versions and approvals. None of those services provides the business-level cost allocation foundation that tagging plus AWS Budgets and Cost Explorer provides.

questions.domain: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.promptHtml: A digital media archive's ML operations team hosts a proprietary content-tagging model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. The inference container image includes all required dependencies, and the inference code only needs the request payload and the local model files at runtime. The security team wants a preventive control that reduces the risk of compromised container code calling external URLs or AWS service APIs from inside the container. Which solution will meet this requirement?
questions.promptText:
A digital media archive's ML operations team hosts a proprietary content-tagging model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. The inference container image includes all required dependencies, and the inference code only needs the request payload and the local model files at runtime. The security team wants a preventive control that reduces the risk of compromised container code calling external URLs or AWS service APIs from inside the container.

Which solution will meet this requirement?

options.text: Enable network isolation for the SageMaker model and keep the inference code independent of outbound service calls.
Attach the endpoint to private subnets and route outbound traffic through a NAT gateway for controlled egress.
Add an S3 gateway VPC endpoint and allow the endpoint role to access only the model artifact bucket.
Enable CloudTrail management events and create an EventBridge rule for SageMaker API changes.

correctText: Enable network isolation for the SageMaker model and keep the inference code independent of outbound service calls.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker network isolation is the preventive control that matches this scenario. When enabled for a SageMaker model, the container cannot make outbound network calls, which helps reduce the blast radius if container code is compromised. This is appropriate only when the container does not need to call Amazon S3, other AWS services, package repositories, license servers, or external APIs during execution.

VPC configuration and private subnets solve a different problem. They let SageMaker-hosted models access resources inside a customer VPC by using subnets and security groups, and they can be paired with VPC endpoints or NAT depending on required connectivity. That is not the same as blocking container egress, and adding a NAT gateway would actually provide an outbound path.

CloudTrail, EventBridge, and endpoint policies are valuable parts of an ML security posture, but they operate at different layers. CloudTrail records API activity for audit, EventBridge can react to events, and S3 endpoint policies can constrain private S3 access. For this requirement, the key distinction is preventive runtime network isolation versus monitoring or selectively routing traffic.

For more detail, see SageMaker network isolation for training and inference containers and Give SageMaker hosted model endpoints access to resources in your VPC.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: A mortgage underwriting team hosts a credit risk model on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. The team has trained a replacement model and wants to evaluate it with live production requests before exposing any customer-facing decisions from the replacement model. The team must compare the candidate model's behavior with the current production model and make a manual promotion decision after reviewing the results. Which deployment approach will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A mortgage underwriting team hosts a credit risk model on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. The team has trained a replacement model and wants to evaluate it with live production requests before exposing any customer-facing decisions from the replacement model. The team must compare the candidate model's behavior with the current production model and make a manual promotion decision after reviewing the results.

Which deployment approach will meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure a SageMaker AI canary deployment for the candidate model.
Configure a SageMaker AI linear deployment for the candidate model.
Configure an all-at-once blue/green deployment for the candidate model.
Configure a SageMaker AI shadow test for the candidate model.

correctText: Configure a SageMaker AI shadow test for the candidate model.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker AI shadow testing is designed for situations where a team wants to evaluate a new model against real production traffic without letting that model influence production responses. The production variant continues to serve client requests, while the candidate variant receives copied traffic for observation and comparison. This helps catch issues that offline validation might miss, especially when real-world request patterns differ from training and test data.

Deployment guardrails such as canary, linear, and all-at-once blue/green deployments are rollout strategies, not passive comparison strategies. They are useful when the team is ready to expose the new model to some or all users while monitoring for problems and possibly rolling back. For this scenario, the key distinction is that the team wants evaluation before exposure, so a shadow test is the safer fit. For more information, see SageMaker AI deployment guardrails and Deploy models for real-time inference.

questions.domain: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.promptHtml: A maritime logistics provider's route optimization team hosts a vessel arrival time model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. The team needs to monitor live inference activity for request volume, response latency, and endpoint instance resource pressure. The team also needs automated notifications when these operational indicators exceed thresholds. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
A maritime logistics provider's route optimization team hosts a vessel arrival time model on an Amazon SageMaker real-time endpoint. The team needs to monitor live inference activity for request volume, response latency, and endpoint instance resource pressure. The team also needs automated notifications when these operational indicators exceed thresholds.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Create AWS Config rules for the SageMaker endpoint configuration. Configure remediation actions when the endpoint becomes noncompliant.
Enable SageMaker Model Monitor data quality checks on captured inference data. Configure violation reports to trigger Amazon SNS notifications.
Enable AWS CloudTrail Insights for the account. Configure EventBridge rules to notify Amazon SNS when unusual write activity is detected.
Create Amazon CloudWatch dashboards and alarms for SageMaker endpoint invocation, latency, and resource metrics. Send alarm notifications through Amazon SNS.

correctText: Create Amazon CloudWatch dashboards and alarms for SageMaker endpoint invocation, latency, and resource metrics. Send alarm notifications through Amazon SNS.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon CloudWatch is the best fit when the monitoring goal is operational health: how many requests an endpoint receives, how long inference takes, whether errors are increasing, and whether the hosting resources are under pressure. SageMaker integrates with CloudWatch so teams can build dashboards and alarms without writing a custom metrics collection system. See Monitor Amazon SageMaker with Amazon CloudWatch.

SageMaker Model Monitor solves a different class of inference monitoring problem. It helps detect data quality drift, model quality degradation, bias drift, and feature attribution drift by comparing captured production inference data against a baseline. That is valuable for model behavior monitoring, but it is not the lowest overhead answer when the requirement is endpoint traffic, latency, and resource monitoring. See Monitor data and model quality with Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor.

CloudTrail and AWS Config are governance tools, not endpoint performance monitoring tools. CloudTrail records API activity for audit and investigation, while AWS Config tracks resource configuration and compliance over time. They can complement an ML operations environment, but CloudWatch is the service that aligns with live inference metrics and threshold-based alarms.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: A renewable energy utility's forecasting platform team updates a demand forecasting model every day. The workflow validates new files in Amazon S3, runs an AWS Glue transformation, queries reference data with Amazon Athena, runs Amazon SageMaker AI processing and training jobs, and loads summary results to Amazon Redshift for analysts. The team wants a managed scheduler for Python-defined dependency graphs that can coordinate ML, ETL, analytics, storage, and database tasks in one place. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
A renewable energy utility's forecasting platform team updates a demand forecasting model every day. The workflow validates new files in Amazon S3, runs an AWS Glue transformation, queries reference data with Amazon Athena, runs Amazon SageMaker AI processing and training jobs, and loads summary results to Amazon Redshift for analysts. The team wants a managed scheduler for Python-defined dependency graphs that can coordinate ML, ETL, analytics, storage, and database tasks in one place.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Use Amazon SageMaker Pipelines to define SageMaker steps that coordinate the data, ML, and reporting tasks.
Use Amazon EventBridge rules to invoke targets that coordinate the data, ML, and reporting tasks.
Use Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow to run scheduled Python DAGs that coordinate the data, ML, and reporting tasks.
Use AWS CodePipeline to create CI/CD stages that coordinate the daily data, ML, and reporting tasks.

correctText: Use Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow to run scheduled Python DAGs that coordinate the data, ML, and reporting tasks.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon MWAA is the best fit when the workflow is broader than the SageMaker model lifecycle and needs to coordinate many kinds of tasks in a scheduled dependency graph. Airflow DAGs are Python code, and Amazon MWAA provides a managed environment for running those DAGs without requiring the team to operate its own Airflow schedulers, workers, and web server. See Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow Documentation and Working with DAGs on Amazon MWAA.

SageMaker Pipelines is purpose-built for ML workflows, especially steps such as preprocessing, training, evaluation, model registration, and deployment. It is excellent when the workflow is centered on SageMaker and benefits from ML lineage and Studio integration, but this scenario emphasizes one orchestrator for ETL, analytics, databases, and ML together. The relevant SageMaker workflow model is described in Amazon SageMaker Pipelines and Define a Pipeline.

Event routing is not the same as workflow orchestration. EventBridge can start work when an event or schedule occurs, and Step Functions can integrate with SageMaker jobs, but the stated requirement is a managed Python DAG scheduler for a mixed data and ML platform. Using many EventBridge rules as a substitute for a DAG orchestrator is harder to reason about, test, and maintain as dependencies grow.

questions.promptHtml: A clinical genomics lab's ML team is training an XGBoost classifier in Amazon SageMaker to flag sequencing samples that require manual variant review. The model reaches very high accuracy on the training data, but the validation accuracy is much lower. The team wants to keep using XGBoost and improve performance on unseen samples. Which action should the team take?
questions.promptText:
A clinical genomics lab's ML team is training an XGBoost classifier in Amazon SageMaker to flag sequencing samples that require manual variant review. The model reaches very high accuracy on the training data, but the validation accuracy is much lower. The team wants to keep using XGBoost and improve performance on unseen samples.

Which action should the team take?

options.text: Tune XGBoost to use deeper trees and weaker L1 or L2 regularization.
Select the candidate model by minimizing training error and ignoring validation metrics.
Tune XGBoost to use shallower trees and stronger L1 or L2 regularization.
Duplicate the training dataset, shuffle the copies, and retrain with more boosting rounds.

correctText: Tune XGBoost to use shallower trees and stronger L1 or L2 regularization.
questions.explanationHtml:
A model with high training accuracy and much lower validation accuracy is usually overfitting. The model has learned details of the training data that do not transfer well to unseen samples. In tree-based boosted models such as XGBoost, overfitting is often controlled by limiting tree complexity and applying regularization.

For SageMaker XGBoost, parameters such as max_depth affect how complex each tree can become, while alpha and lambda provide L1 and L2 regularization. Shallower trees and stronger regularization trade some training-set fit for better generalization, which is the right tradeoff when validation performance is lagging. The AWS documentation lists these XGBoost hyperparameters in XGBoost Hyperparameters.

Validation data is central to this decision because it estimates performance on data that was not used to fit the model. Selecting only by training error, duplicating existing records, or increasing model capacity are anti-patterns when the observed problem is overfitting. SageMaker guidance on validation and training curves is covered in Evaluate Your Model and Training and Validation Curves.

questions.promptHtml: A city transportation authority's data platform team is beginning an ML initiative to improve maintenance planning. The team receives nightly CSV exports from ticketing systems, JSON telemetry from vehicles, and image files from inspection crews. Future ML use cases are not fully defined. The team wants to keep the original records, support low-cost storage at scale, and make the data discoverable for SQL-based exploration without maintaining database servers. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
A city transportation authority's data platform team is beginning an ML initiative to improve maintenance planning. The team receives nightly CSV exports from ticketing systems, JSON telemetry from vehicles, and image files from inspection crews. Future ML use cases are not fully defined. The team wants to keep the original records, support low-cost storage at scale, and make the data discoverable for SQL-based exploration without maintaining database servers.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Mount Amazon EFS to SageMaker notebooks, write files by source type, and track schemas in notebook repositories.
Store each feed in Amazon S3 in its native format, run AWS Glue crawlers, and use Amazon Athena for exploration.
Create SageMaker Feature Store feature groups, load raw records into the online store, and query features for training.
Transform each feed into a fixed star schema, load it into Amazon Redshift, and use Redshift for exploration.

correctText: Store each feed in Amazon S3 in its native format, run AWS Glue crawlers, and use Amazon Athena for exploration.
questions.explanationHtml:
For early-stage ML data collection with mixed structured, semi-structured, and unstructured sources, Amazon S3 is commonly used as the durable storage layer because it can hold objects in their native formats at large scale. This fits the requirement to preserve original records and avoid committing too early to a rigid schema. See Amazon S3 fundamentals for the basic bucket, object, and access-control model.

AWS Glue crawlers add the metadata layer that a raw object store does not provide by itself. Crawlers inspect data stores, infer schemas where applicable, and create or update tables in the AWS Glue Data Catalog, as described in AWS Glue crawlers. Query engines can then use the catalog to explore data without first loading everything into a managed data warehouse.

The important design tradeoff is schema-on-read versus schema-on-write. A data warehouse such as Redshift is useful when data is structured, curated, and optimized for known business intelligence queries.
