A data lake pattern is better when raw data must be retained for future ML feature engineering, especially when the team does not yet know which fields or file types will become valuable.

questions.promptHtml: A wildlife conservation nonprofit's ML team is building a model in Amazon SageMaker AI for trail-camera images. A single image can contain multiple animals of different species in different parts of the frame. The team wants the model to identify each animal occurrence, return a species category and confidence score for each occurrence, and reduce training effort by starting from pretrained network weights. Which solution will best meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A wildlife conservation nonprofit's ML team is building a model in Amazon SageMaker AI for trail-camera images. A single image can contain multiple animals of different species in different parts of the frame. The team wants the model to identify each animal occurrence, return a species category and confidence score for each occurrence, and reduce training effort by starting from pretrained network weights.

Which solution will best meet these requirements?

options.text: Train an Amazon Rekognition Custom Labels model on the labeled images from Amazon S3.
Train the SageMaker AI Object Detection algorithm in transfer learning mode on the labeled images.
Train the SageMaker AI Image Classification algorithm in transfer learning mode on the labeled images.
Train the SageMaker AI K-Means algorithm on image embeddings extracted from the labeled images.

correctText: Train the SageMaker AI Object Detection algorithm in transfer learning mode on the labeled images.
questions.explanationHtml:
When an image can contain multiple occurrences of objects and the output must include a category and confidence score for each occurrence, the problem is not ordinary image-level classification. A classifier answers a question such as, what is the main class of this image? An object detection model answers a richer question: what objects are present, and where are they?

In SageMaker AI, the built-in object detection algorithm is appropriate for images that contain multiple objects. The course material highlights that the MXNet variant uses a CNN with Single Shot multibox Detector (SSD), can use VGG-16 or ResNet-50 as the base CNN, and supports transfer learning by using pretrained base network weights instead of random initial weights. This makes it a practical fit when the team has labeled images and wants to reduce training effort.

Transfer learning is useful because lower layers of a computer vision network often learn general visual features, such as edges, textures, and shapes. Reusing pretrained weights lets the training job focus more of its learning on the domain-specific species categories rather than learning all visual representations from scratch.

The broader SageMaker AI documentation maps problem types to algorithm choices and distinguishes supervised, unsupervised, and other ML approaches. See Use SageMaker built-in algorithms or pretrained models and Choose an algorithm for the general SageMaker AI algorithm selection framework.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: A professional sports league's analytics engineering team uses AWS CodePipeline to deploy infrastructure for a model scoring service. The pipeline currently has a Source stage that pulls application code and an AWS CloudFormation Deploy stage that creates the service resources. The team adds unit tests and a packaging step that creates deployment files required by the CloudFormation template. The Deploy stage now fails because it can only access files from the original source package. The team wants a managed solution that shows where failures occur in the release process. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A professional sports league's analytics engineering team uses AWS CodePipeline to deploy infrastructure for a model scoring service. The pipeline currently has a Source stage that pulls application code and an AWS CloudFormation Deploy stage that creates the service resources. The team adds unit tests and a packaging step that creates deployment files required by the CloudFormation template. The Deploy stage now fails because it can only access files from the original source package. The team wants a managed solution that shows where failures occur in the release process.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Add a CodeBuild action in a Build stage after Source, define buildspec commands for tests and packaging, and configure the deploy action to use the CodeBuild output artifact.
Invoke CodeBuild from an EventBridge rule on repository changes, define buildspec commands for tests and packaging, and keep CodePipeline starting at the deploy stage.
Add a CodeBuild action in a Test stage after Deploy, define buildspec commands for tests and packaging, and keep the deploy action using the Source output artifact.
Create a CodeDeploy deployment group for the service, move tests and packaging into deployment hooks, and configure CodePipeline to deploy the original Source output artifact.

correctText: Add a CodeBuild action in a Build stage after Source, define buildspec commands for tests and packaging, and configure the deploy action to use the CodeBuild output artifact.
questions.explanationHtml:
CodePipeline is the orchestration layer for CI/CD workflows. A pipeline is organized into stages such as source, build, test, provision, and deploy, and each stage contains actions that consume and produce artifacts. In this scenario, the deployment depends on files that are not present in the original source artifact, so the pipeline needs a managed build action that creates a new artifact before deployment.

CodeBuild is the appropriate service for compiling code, running tests, and producing ready-to-deploy packages. The build commands and artifact paths are defined in a buildspec.yml file, and the CodeBuild action in CodePipeline can expose the build output as an artifact for a later deploy action. This keeps the flow traceable because failures are visible in the specific stage or action that failed.

Running the build after deployment reverses the dependency order. Triggering CodeBuild outside the pipeline can be useful in other event-driven workflows, but it weakens the managed artifact handoff that CodePipeline provides. CodeDeploy is also not the right substitute for a build stage when the problem is generating files that the CloudFormation deploy action must consume.

For more information, see CodePipeline concepts, CodeBuild action reference in CodePipeline, and CodeBuild buildspec reference.

questions.promptHtml: A regional airline's workforce analytics team is preparing a labeled training dataset for an Amazon SageMaker model that predicts whether crew members are likely to exceed monthly overtime thresholds. Before any model is trained, the compliance team wants evidence about whether the existing labels are distributed differently across employee groups. The team does not need per-record feature contribution explanations at this stage. Which action should the ML engineer take?
questions.promptText:
A regional airline's workforce analytics team is preparing a labeled training dataset for an Amazon SageMaker model that predicts whether crew members are likely to exceed monthly overtime thresholds. Before any model is trained, the compliance team wants evidence about whether the existing labels are distributed differently across employee groups. The team does not need per-record feature contribution explanations at this stage.

Which action should the ML engineer take?

options.text: Run SageMaker Clarify post-training bias analysis after batch inference completes.
Run SageMaker Clarify pre-training bias analysis on the labeled training dataset.
Configure SageMaker Model Monitor feature attribution drift checks on the endpoint.
Run SageMaker Clarify SHAP explainability analysis on generated model predictions.

correctText: Run SageMaker Clarify pre-training bias analysis on the labeled training dataset.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker Clarify supports different analysis goals at different points in the ML lifecycle. When the question is about the dataset before a model is trained, the relevant category is pre-training bias. This helps teams inspect whether the source labels or feature distributions show potential imbalance across groups before the model has a chance to learn those patterns.

Post-training bias analysis requires model predictions, so it is appropriate after a trained model has produced outputs. SHAP-based explainability is also prediction-focused, it estimates how much each feature contributed to a model output. Those are valuable for model insight, but they do not satisfy a pre-training requirement about existing label distributions.

Model Monitor is part of the production monitoring story. It can help detect drift after deployment, including data quality, model quality, bias drift, and feature attribution drift when configured appropriately. That is a different operational phase than evaluating a labeled training dataset before model development proceeds.

For more detail, see the SageMaker Clarify documentation for pre-training bias metrics, post-training bias metrics, and SHAP feature attributions.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: A specialty pharmacy's ML platform team is deploying two Amazon SageMaker AI models. The first model, the adherence model, supports a pharmacist-facing application that needs low-latency, interactive predictions and cannot tolerate cold starts. Request volume varies during the day. The second model, the audit model, scores a full dataset in Amazon S3 once each night and does not need a hosted endpoint between scoring runs. Which TWO actions should the team take?
questions.promptText:
A specialty pharmacy's ML platform team is deploying two Amazon SageMaker AI models. The first model, the adherence model, supports a pharmacist-facing application that needs low-latency, interactive predictions and cannot tolerate cold starts. Request volume varies during the day. The second model, the audit model, scores a full dataset in Amazon S3 once each night and does not need a hosted endpoint between scoring runs.

Which TWO actions should the team take?

options.text: Deploy the adherence model to a SageMaker asynchronous endpoint and have the app wait for queued results.
Deploy the adherence model to a SageMaker serverless endpoint and accept cold starts after idle periods.
Run the audit model with SageMaker Batch Transform and store the nightly prediction results in Amazon S3.
Deploy the audit model to a SageMaker real-time endpoint and keep it active between nightly scoring windows.
Deploy the adherence model to a SageMaker real-time endpoint and configure autoscaling for changing request volume.

correctText: Run the audit model with SageMaker Batch Transform and store the nightly prediction results in Amazon S3.
Deploy the adherence model to a SageMaker real-time endpoint and configure autoscaling for changing request volume.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker AI inference options are chosen primarily by the response pattern, not only by the model type. A real-time endpoint is appropriate when an application sends individual inference requests and needs a low-latency response while a user or transaction is waiting. If demand changes over time, endpoint autoscaling can help right-size provisioned capacity for that endpoint.

Batch Transform is different because it is job oriented. The service reads input data, commonly from Amazon S3, produces predictions for the dataset, and writes results back to storage without requiring a persistent endpoint to sit idle between runs. That makes it a better match for scheduled offline scoring than a continuously hosted endpoint.

Serverless Inference is useful when traffic is intermittent and the workload can tolerate cold starts, but that tradeoff conflicts with a strict interactive latency requirement. Asynchronous Inference is useful when requests can be queued, often because payloads are large or processing takes longer, but it is not the right pattern when the application must wait for an immediate response. For more detail, see Deploy models for inference, Real-time inference, Asynchronous inference, and Batch transform.

questions.promptHtml: An online education provider's ML team is preparing tabular learner activity data for a course completion model. The raw data is stored in Amazon S3 and includes email addresses, phone numbers, and free-form support notes. Analysts need a visual workflow to identify sensitive fields and create reusable masking or deletion steps before the data is shared. Data scientists also need a SageMaker-native visual workflow to inspect feature distributions, handle missing values and outliers, and quickly estimate whether the transformed features have predictive signal before exporting the preparation logic. Which TWO actions will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
An online education provider's ML team is preparing tabular learner activity data for a course completion model. The raw data is stored in Amazon S3 and includes email addresses, phone numbers, and free-form support notes. Analysts need a visual workflow to identify sensitive fields and create reusable masking or deletion steps before the data is shared. Data scientists also need a SageMaker-native visual workflow to inspect feature distributions, handle missing values and outliers, and quickly estimate whether the transformed features have predictive signal before exporting the preparation logic.

Which TWO actions will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a SageMaker Data Wrangler flow, review visual feature summaries, apply built-in transforms, and use Quick Model before export.
Create an AWS Glue DataBrew project, run a profile job with PII statistics, and save a recipe that masks or deletes sensitive fields.
Create an AWS Glue crawler, catalog the S3 data, query the tables with Athena, and save SQL views for downstream model training.
Create SageMaker Feature Store feature groups, ingest the raw records, and query the offline store with Athena for training data.
Create an Amazon QuickSight analysis, add calculated fields and anomaly insights, and export dashboard results for model training.

correctText: Create a SageMaker Data Wrangler flow, review visual feature summaries, apply built-in transforms, and use Quick Model before export.
Create an AWS Glue DataBrew project, run a profile job with PII statistics, and save a recipe that masks or deletes sensitive fields.
questions.explanationHtml:
AWS Glue DataBrew and SageMaker Data Wrangler address different parts of this preparation workflow. DataBrew is a visual preparation service for datasets, recipes, profile jobs, and jobs, and it is well suited when the team must identify PII and apply repeatable obfuscation or deletion steps before sharing data. See AWS Glue DataBrew core concepts and terms.

SageMaker Data Wrangler is more ML-focused. It helps data scientists import data, analyze and visualize features, apply transformations, and export preparation flows into the SageMaker workflow. The course material also emphasizes Quick Model as a practical way to test whether preparation choices are improving the downstream model signal before committing to a full training workflow. See Overview of Amazon SageMaker Data Wrangler and SageMaker Data Wrangler transforms.

A Glue crawler plus Athena is useful for schema discovery and SQL querying over S3, but it is not a substitute for visual PII remediation or SageMaker-native feature preparation. QuickSight is primarily for dashboards and business analytics, so using it as the main ETL and ML feature preparation tool is the wrong tradeoff. Feature Store becomes valuable after features are defined and need reuse or consistency, but it does not perform the requested visual exploration and transformation work by itself.

questions.domain: Deployment and Orchestration of ML Workflows
questions.promptHtml: A video game studio's personalization platform team runs a containerized feature enrichment service on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate. A networking CloudFormation stack already provisions the private subnets and security group that the service must use. The networking stack must remain independently updated from the Fargate service stack, and both stacks are deployed in the same AWS account and Region. The team wants repeatable infrastructure deployments and wants to avoid manually copying resource identifiers between stacks. Which approach will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
A video game studio's personalization platform team runs a containerized feature enrichment service on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate. A networking CloudFormation stack already provisions the private subnets and security group that the service must use. The networking stack must remain independently updated from the Fargate service stack, and both stacks are deployed in the same AWS account and Region. The team wants repeatable infrastructure deployments and wants to avoid manually copying resource identifiers between stacks.

Which approach will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Move the network resources into a nested stack, and deploy the service stack as the parent stack.
Create duplicate network resources in the service stack, and configure the service to use those resources.
Add Parameters for the network values, and paste the current identifiers into each service deployment.
Add exported Outputs for the network values, and use Fn::ImportValue in the Fargate service stack.

correctText: Add exported Outputs for the network values, and use Fn::ImportValue in the Fargate service stack.
questions.explanationHtml:
AWS CloudFormation is designed to model infrastructure as templates and provision those resources as stacks. When one independently managed stack needs values from another stack in the same account and Region, a common pattern is to publish values in the producer stack's Outputs section and import them in the consumer stack with Fn::ImportValue.

This pattern is useful for ML workflow infrastructure because different teams often own different layers, such as networking, container compute, model hosting, or CI/CD. The networking stack can own private subnets and security groups, while the ECS Fargate service stack consumes those values without hard-coding identifiers. The result is repeatable provisioning with clearer ownership boundaries.

Parameters are valid CloudFormation inputs, but using them by manually pasting generated IDs is an operational anti-pattern when the value is already managed by another stack. Nested stacks are better when resources share a parent lifecycle, not when an existing platform stack must remain separately updated. Creating duplicate resources avoids the reference problem only by ignoring the requirement to use the shared resources.

For more information, see the CloudFormation overview in CloudFormation overview, the Outputs section syntax, and the Fn::ImportValue reference.

questions.domain: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.promptHtml: A digital advertising network's ML operations team deploys Amazon SageMaker endpoints and endpoint configurations in several AWS Regions. The team needs a retained audit record that shows which IAM principals create, update, and delete these resources. The team also wants to analyze the records later during investigations. The team does not need Amazon S3 object-level access records or AWS Lambda invocation records. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A digital advertising network's ML operations team deploys Amazon SageMaker endpoints and endpoint configurations in several AWS Regions. The team needs a retained audit record that shows which IAM principals create, update, and delete these resources. The team also wants to analyze the records later during investigations. The team does not need Amazon S3 object-level access records or AWS Lambda invocation records.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Create a multi-Region CloudTrail trail that logs management events, deliver the logs to Amazon S3, and query the S3 logs with Athena.
Create a single-Region CloudTrail trail that logs data events, deliver the logs to CloudWatch Logs, and query the log group.
Create CloudWatch dashboards for SageMaker endpoint metrics, export endpoint logs to Amazon S3, and query the S3 logs with Athena.
Create AWS Config recorders in each Region, deliver configuration snapshots to Amazon S3, and query the S3 data with Athena.

correctText: Create a multi-Region CloudTrail trail that logs management events, deliver the logs to Amazon S3, and query the S3 logs with Athena.
questions.explanationHtml:
CloudTrail trails are the AWS mechanism for retaining an audit history of API activity in an account. For changes to resources such as SageMaker endpoints, endpoint configurations, IAM policies, VPC resources, and logging configuration, the relevant category is typically management events. These events record control plane activity from the AWS Management Console, AWS CLI, SDKs, and AWS services.

A trail can deliver events to Amazon S3, which is the practical choice when the team needs retention beyond the default event history period and wants later investigation workflows. Once the logs are in S3, a team can use services such as Athena to query them without loading the data into a separate database. A multi-Region trail is the right operational choice when the resources are deployed in several Regions because it avoids gaps caused by only collecting activity from one Region.

AWS Config answers a different question: what a resource configuration looked like and whether it complied with rules. CloudWatch answers operational questions about metrics, logs, dashboards, and alarms. CloudTrail data events are important for data plane activity such as S3 object access, but they are not the correct event category for the stated SageMaker resource changes. For more information, see Overview of creating trails, CloudTrail EventSelector, and Creating a trail in the CloudTrail console.

questions.promptHtml: A maritime insurance broker's analytics team uses Amazon Transcribe to create transcripts from recorded claims calls. The transcripts frequently misrecognize vessel classes, policy acronyms, and product names. The team has a curated list of these terms and preferred written forms, and wants to improve recognition without training a broader domain language model. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST effort?
questions.promptText:
A maritime insurance broker's analytics team uses Amazon Transcribe to create transcripts from recorded claims calls. The transcripts frequently misrecognize vessel classes, policy acronyms, and product names. The team has a curated list of these terms and preferred written forms, and wants to improve recognition without training a broader domain language model.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST effort?

options.text: Train an Amazon Transcribe custom language model, and use it for the transcription jobs.
Create an Amazon Transcribe custom vocabulary, and apply it to the transcription jobs.
Use Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, and retrieve policy documents during transcript generation.
Build an Amazon Comprehend custom entity recognizer, and run it after each transcript is created.

correctText: Create an Amazon Transcribe custom vocabulary, and apply it to the transcription jobs.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon Transcribe is the appropriate managed AI service when the input is speech and the required output is text. For known terminology such as acronyms, product names, jargon, and uncommon phrases, a custom vocabulary helps the speech recognition system favor those terms in the transcript. This matches the scenario because the team already has a controlled list of terms and preferred written forms.

A custom language model is a heavier option for cases where the service needs to learn broader context from domain-specific text, such as large volumes of specialized language. That can be useful, but it is more work and does not match the requirement to avoid training a broader model. Post-processing with entity extraction can identify terms only if they were transcribed correctly in the first place, so it does not solve the recognition problem at the source.

Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases are designed for retrieval augmented generation, where a foundation model can use proprietary data to generate more grounded responses. That is a different problem from speech-to-text accuracy. For more information, see Amazon Transcribe overview and Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases.

questions.domain: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.promptHtml: A renewable energy utility's ML team trains a demand forecasting model by using distributed Amazon SageMaker AI training jobs. The training dataset contains customer meter readings in Amazon S3, and the trained model artifacts are written back to Amazon S3. The security team requires customer-controlled encryption for stored training data and artifacts, and requires encrypted communication between training containers during distributed training. The solution should require the least change to the training code. Which solution will meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A renewable energy utility's ML team trains a demand forecasting model by using distributed Amazon SageMaker AI training jobs. The training dataset contains customer meter readings in Amazon S3, and the trained model artifacts are written back to Amazon S3. The security team requires customer-controlled encryption for stored training data and artifacts, and requires encrypted communication between training containers during distributed training. The solution should require the least change to the training code.

Which solution will meet these requirements?

options.text: Use AWS CloudTrail for SageMaker AI API auditing, and configure CloudWatch alarms for training job logs and container metrics.
Store an encryption secret in AWS Secrets Manager, and modify the training script to encrypt records before writing artifacts to Amazon S3.
Configure the training data and artifact locations to use a customer managed AWS KMS key, and enable inter-container traffic encryption for the training job.
Enable network isolation for the training job, and use the default TLS settings for all service calls made by the training containers.

correctText: Configure the training data and artifact locations to use a customer managed AWS KMS key, and enable inter-container traffic encryption for the training job.
questions.explanationHtml:
For SageMaker AI training workloads, use the service's built-in security controls before adding custom encryption logic. AWS KMS is the standard AWS service for customer-controlled encryption keys, and SageMaker AI can use KMS keys for data that the service stores as part of jobs and artifacts. Amazon S3 can also store training inputs and outputs encrypted with KMS-managed keys, which keeps encryption centralized and auditable.

Distributed training introduces another path to protect: traffic between training containers. SageMaker AI supports inter-container traffic encryption, also known as inter-node training communication encryption, for training or tuning jobs. This is designed for cases where policy or regulation requires encryption even for communication inside the training cluster, although it can add training time and cost for deep learning workloads.

Network isolation, VPC controls, logging, and auditing remain useful, but they solve different problems. CloudTrail records API activity for audit and investigation, while CloudWatch helps with logs and metrics. Those services do not replace encryption at rest or inter-container encryption. For more information, see SageMaker AI security overview, SageMaker AI encryption at rest, SageMaker AI encryption in transit, and Logging SageMaker AI API calls with AWS CloudTrail.

questions.domain: ML Solution Monitoring, Maintenance, and Security
questions.promptHtml: A telemedicine platform's ML operations team hosts a symptom triage model on an Amazon SageMaker AI serverless endpoint. Traffic is idle overnight and uneven during the day, but requests spike predictably at 8 AM and after lunch. CloudWatch latency alarms occur during the first requests after idle periods, while the monthly inference budget is tight. The team wants to reduce user-visible startup delays without paying for peak capacity continuously. Which action will best meet these requirements?
questions.promptText:
A telemedicine platform's ML operations team hosts a symptom triage model on an Amazon SageMaker AI serverless endpoint. Traffic is idle overnight and uneven during the day, but requests spike predictably at 8 AM and after lunch. CloudWatch latency alarms occur during the first requests after idle periods, while the monthly inference budget is tight. The team wants to reduce user-visible startup delays without paying for peak capacity continuously.

Which action will best meet these requirements?

options.text: Configure Application Auto Scaling for the endpoint's provisioned concurrency with bounded minimum and maximum values that follow expected traffic windows.
Request a SageMaker AI service quota increase for serverless endpoint concurrency before changing the endpoint scaling configuration.
Replace the endpoint with a real-time endpoint that uses a fixed instance count sized for the busiest hour and runs continuously.
Move the inference workload to SageMaker Batch Transform and process accumulated requests on a frequent schedule during the day.

correctText: Configure Application Auto Scaling for the endpoint's provisioned concurrency with bounded minimum and maximum values that follow expected traffic windows.
questions.explanationHtml:
SageMaker AI Serverless Inference is designed for workloads with idle periods or uneven traffic because it avoids managing instances and can reduce cost when requests are infrequent. The tradeoff is that a request after idle time can experience additional startup latency. Provisioned concurrency is a way to keep some serverless capacity ready, and using Application Auto Scaling lets the team adjust that ready capacity instead of paying for peak readiness all day.

The best approach is to put bounds around provisioned concurrency and scale it according to expected demand, such as known morning and lunch spikes. This does not promise that every latency spike disappears, but it directly targets the cost and performance tension in the scenario. For SageMaker endpoint scaling policies, see SageMaker AI endpoint auto scaling policy overview, and for serverless provisioned concurrency scaling, see How to use Application Auto Scaling to scale SageMaker Serverless Inference Provisioned Concurrency.

A fixed real-time endpoint can be appropriate for consistently low-latency, steady traffic, but running capacity sized for peak demand conflicts with the tight budget and idle overnight pattern. A service quota increase is useful only when quota limits are the bottleneck, and the scenario gives no evidence of quota errors. Batch Transform is the wrong inference mode for an interactive application because it is designed for processing datasets asynchronously rather than responding to individual user requests.

questions.promptHtml: A national museum consortium's ML data engineering team collects JSON interaction events from exhibit kiosks for nightly recommendation model training. Producers currently write to an Amazon Kinesis Data Streams stream in provisioned mode, and a custom consumer buffers records to Amazon S3. During major exhibition openings, producers are throttled, but the team does not need replay capability, long-term stream retention, or custom stream consumers. The team wants to deliver the events to Amazon S3 with the least operational effort. Which action should the team take?
questions.promptText:
A national museum consortium's ML data engineering team collects JSON interaction events from exhibit kiosks for nightly recommendation model training. Producers currently write to an Amazon Kinesis Data Streams stream in provisioned mode, and a custom consumer buffers records to Amazon S3. During major exhibition openings, producers are throttled, but the team does not need replay capability, long-term stream retention, or custom stream consumers. The team wants to deliver the events to Amazon S3 with the least operational effort.

Which action should the team take?

options.text: Send the events to Amazon Data Firehose and configure an Amazon S3 destination.
Process the events with Managed Service for Apache Flink and write the results to Amazon S3.
Increase the shard count for the Kinesis Data Streams stream and retain the custom consumer.
Move the events to Amazon MSK and configure Kafka producers and consumers.

correctText: Send the events to Amazon Data Firehose and configure an Amazon S3 destination.
questions.explanationHtml:
Amazon Data Firehose is the best fit when the workload is streaming ingestion into destinations such as Amazon S3, Amazon Redshift, Amazon OpenSearch Service, third-party services, or an HTTP endpoint, and the team wants a managed delivery path. Firehose buffers records based on size or time and handles much of the scaling and delivery management for near real-time ingestion, which is a good tradeoff for nightly ML training data collection where subsecond processing and replay are not required. See the Firehose quota and scaling considerations in Amazon Data Firehose Quotas.

Kinesis Data Streams is a better fit when applications need real-time producer and consumer code, stream retention, and replay from the same source records. In provisioned mode, capacity planning is tied to shards, so simply increasing shard count can address throughput pressure but does not remove the operational responsibility that the team wants to avoid. The quota model for streams is described in Amazon Kinesis Data Streams Quotas and Limits.

Amazon MSK and Managed Service for Apache Flink are both plausible streaming technologies, but they solve different problems. MSK is useful for Kafka-based producer and consumer ecosystems, while Flink is useful for custom stream processing logic. For this scenario, the simplest scalable ingestion pattern is managed delivery into S3, not building or operating another stream-processing application.

questions.promptHtml: A semiconductor fabrication plant's yield engineering team trains an Amazon SageMaker Linear Learner binary classifier to predict whether wafers will pass inspection. The dataset contains hundreds of normalized sensor-derived features, and the team believes many of the features add noise. The model performs well on training data but is inconsistent on validation data. The team wants to improve generalization while keeping the same simple linear modeling approach. Which action should the ML engineer take?
questions.promptText:
A semiconductor fabrication plant's yield engineering team trains an Amazon SageMaker Linear Learner binary classifier to predict whether wafers will pass inspection. The dataset contains hundreds of normalized sensor-derived features, and the team believes many of the features add noise. The model performs well on training data but is inconsistent on validation data. The team wants to improve generalization while keeping the same simple linear modeling approach.

Which action should the ML engineer take?

options.text: Replace the linear model with additional hidden layers before tuning.
Increase the Linear Learner l1 regularization hyperparameter during tuning.
Switch to a neural-network estimator solely to apply dropout regularization.
Decrease the Linear Learner l1 regularization hyperparameter during tuning.

correctText: Increase the Linear Learner l1 regularization hyperparameter during tuning.
questions.explanationHtml:
Regularization is used to constrain a model so it does not rely too heavily on patterns that appear only in the training data. When a linear model has many features and some are likely noisy, L1 regularization is often a strong fit because it can push less useful feature weights toward zero, which has a feature-selection effect while keeping the model simple.

L2 regularization, often called weight decay, is also useful for controlling overfitting because it discourages large weights and can make the model more stable. In this scenario, the requirement points specifically to a simple linear model with many noisy or weakly relevant features, so increasing l1 is the most targeted action among the available choices.

Decreasing regularization moves in the wrong direction because it gives the model more freedom to fit noisy training patterns. Dropout is valuable in neural networks, but switching model families solely to use dropout does not preserve the stated linear modeling approach. Adding hidden layers similarly increases complexity and can increase variance when the model already performs better on training data than on validation data.

The AWS certification outline explicitly includes the benefits of regularization techniques such as dropout, weight decay, L1, and L2 in Domain 2: AWS Certified Machine Learning Engineer - Associate Domain 2. The SageMaker Linear Learner documentation lists l1 for L1 regularization and wd for weight decay, or L2 regularization: Linear Learner Hyperparameters. AWS also describes regularization as a way to address overfitting in Model Fit: Underfitting vs. Overfitting.

The lab wants to receive a notification when monthly actual spend reaches a defined threshold. The lab also wants to scope the cost tracking to the sandbox ML activity by using services and resource tags. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
questions.promptText:
An agricultural robotics lab's ML engineering team uses a sandbox AWS account for Amazon SageMaker notebooks, Amazon EMR experiments, and occasional Amazon EC2 test instances. The lab wants to receive a notification when monthly actual spend reaches a defined threshold. The lab also wants to scope the cost tracking to the sandbox ML activity by using services and resource tags.

Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Review AWS Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks weekly, export the findings, and manually notify engineers about idle resources.
Create a CloudWatch dashboard for SageMaker and EC2 metrics, configure alarms, and use the alarms to track utilization trends.
Create an AWS Budgets cost budget with an actual-cost threshold, apply service and tag filters, and configure budget notifications.
Create an AWS Cost Explorer report grouped by service, enable monthly forecasts, and share the report with the engineering managers.

correctText: Create an AWS Budgets cost budget with an actual-cost threshold, apply service and tag filters, and configure budget notifications.
questions.explanationHtml:
AWS Budgets is the most direct service for defining cost or usage budgets and sending notifications when actual or forecasted values cross a threshold. In this scenario, the team needs a low-overhead way to track monthly sandbox spending and alert the right people, so a cost budget with service and tag filters fits the requirement. See the AWS Budgets overview.

AWS Cost Explorer helps engineers understand where money is going by analyzing historical cost and usage, building reports, and reviewing forecasts. That makes it useful for investigation and planning, but it is not the simplest choice when the primary requirement is a threshold-based notification. The AWS Cost Explorer overview describes its role as an analysis and forecasting service.

AWS Trusted Advisor is valuable for account-level recommendations, including cost optimization checks for idle or underutilized resources. However, it is recommendation-oriented rather than budget-threshold-oriented, so it does not satisfy the notification requirement as directly as AWS Budgets. The AWS Trusted Advisor overview and Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks documentation are useful for understanding that role.
